article_text:
Patrick Flores and Chris Lee, respectively the chief curator and assistant chief executive of the National Gallery Singapore, will leave the institution in December, The Strait Times reports.

Their departure will coincide with that of chief executive Eugene Tan who announced in September that he would be stepping down. Chng Hak-Peng will be taking over Tan’s role. Details have yet to be announced regarding the positions of chief curator and assistant chief executive.

article_text:
Taschen publishes Life. Let’s Dance by Lyndsey Winship, edited by Reuel Golden . Lyndsey Winship writes.

I wanna dance with somebody. Decades of dance in the archives of Life.

Let’s storm the stage with Life magazine, through the finest vintage dance photographs taken around the world! From rumba to twist, jitterbug to waltz, lindy hop to flamenco, Eastern dances to ballet, and disco to tap, with legends of the genre such as Martha Graham, the Rockettes, Fred Astaire and Rudolf Nureyev.

When publisher Henry R. Luce founded Life in 1936, his aim was “to see life, to see the world, to eyewitness great events.” Life devotes its sixth issue to the world of dance, acknowledging its communal and cultural importance, beyond the joy the art form represents. From scenes in Las Vegas or Hollywood to Woodstock and the nightclubs of Paris, from the provinces of western China to the ballrooms of Harlem, Let’s Dance traces the evolution and impact of dance, immortalized by Life photographers between the late 1930s and the early 1970s.

With more than 200 often previously unpublished images, scanned from original negatives drawn from Life ’s vast archives, every page of Let’s Dance evokes a defining era, an important dance style, a leading dancer, a legendary choreographer or a glamorous star, sometimes all in a single shot. Among the subjects whirling through this book are modern dance pioneer Martha Graham, stars Rudolf Nureyev and Margot Fonteyn, Fred Astaire, Sammy Davis Jr, Elvis Presley swiveling his hips onstage, and Brigitte Bardot barefoot in the dust in Spain. Let’s Dance doesn’t show only professionals and celebrities, but also unknowns and amateurs who love to dance, such as couples in a South Carolina dance hall, pupils in a ballet class in Suriname, Indigenous dancers in India, Greece, Senegal and Mexico, the disco kids of the 1960s, square dance enthusiasts in Oklahoma, shy debutantes, or Princeton students letting off steam at the end of the year.

Besides these expertly chosen archive photographs, Let’s Dance includes Life covers and tear-out pages, as well as an introductory essay and explanatory captions by dance critic Lyndsey Winship, which recall the historical context of the images. At some 250 pages, Let’s Dance offers not just a history of this thrilling performing art, but also an evocation of the childlike delight and catharsis that dance provides. It makes you want to get up, dance and have the time of your life.

About the author

Lyndsey Winship is the dance critic at The Guardian. She has previously written about dance for Time Out London, The Independent, The Times, the Daily Telegraph, the Evening Standard and Dance magazine. She is the author of Being a Dancer, published by Nick Hern Books.

About the editor

Reuel Golden, former editor-in-chief of the British Journal of Photography, is the editor of TASCHEN’s photography titles, including Mick Rock: The Rise of David Bowie, New York and London from the “Portrait of a City” series, Andy Warhol. Polaroids, The Rolling Stones, Her Majesty, the books on National Geographic and David Bailey SUMO.

article_text:
株式会社リクルートホールディングスが運営するBUGでは、2026年10月14日（水）より、藤岡亜弥個展「Forget Me Not」を開催します。1996年に自らの日常を写した「なみだ壺」で BUGの前身であるガーディアン・ガーデン主催の「写真[人間の街]プロジェクト」に参加。2005年に移民としてブラジルに渡った祖母にまつわる「離愁」で「第24回写真『ひとつぼ展』」に入選、2017年には個展「アヤ子、形而上学的研究」を開催するなどリクルートがデビュー当時からキャリアを応援してきたアーティストです。

本展は国内外で活躍する藤岡がBUGとのコミッションで新シリーズを展開。藤岡は9年前にオーストラリア・メルボルン在住の女性から、ある日本人女性の存在をめぐる一通のDM（ダイレクトメッセージ）を受け取ります。地元である広島・呉から遠く離れたオーストラリア、その二つの都市の戦後から現在までをつらぬく、まさしく「事実は小説よりも奇妙なり」というべき、めくればめくるほど謎が増してゆく制作がスタートしました。

サンパウロで祖母の軌跡を追う「離愁」、ヨーロッパを旅した「さよならを教えて」、5年過ごしたニューヨーク生活で生まれた「Life Studies」などこれまでのシリーズと違わず、今回も導かれるように世界を旅し、ファインダーから物語を編み出す藤岡の新機軸を打ち出す展覧会です。

新シリーズ、撮り下ろし、映像作品への初挑戦

本展の軸となるのは藤岡が初めて挑戦した映像作品を含んだ撮り下ろしによる新シリーズ《Forget Me Not》。 3年の構想・制作期間の本作で取り扱うのは、実際に自身の身に起きた未解決のできごとです。当事者として、自身もどのようになるか分からないできごとの現実が刻一刻と自分の選択とシャッターによって切り拓かれていくさまは、ドキュメンタリーでもルポルタージュでもなく、「①作者は作品の中に登場すべきではない／②選択によって作者の見解を示す／③創作的処理を必要とする」*というノンフィクション・ノヴェルの特色と重なります。 写真という決定的な事実に即したものを提示しながら、感情をかき立てるストーリーとしても提示するというアンビバレントな方法にて展覧会はつくられます。

呉とメルボルン、そしてサンパウロを結ぶ女たちの人生

藤岡の出身地である広島県は海外への移民送出の数が全国1位でした。藤岡の祖母も移民2世としてブラジルで生まれ、親が買った宝くじが偶然当たり、20歳のときに家族で再び日本に、広島・呉に戻ることになりました。その祖母、フジオカキミエと一文字違いのフジオカキミコを探すオーストラリア・メルボルン在住のとある女性から届いたメッセージから、祖母ではないその一文字違いの女性は誰か、 という謎解きをするために藤岡は呉とメルボルンに向かいます。 実在するかどうかも分からないキミコを探す旅は、さまざまな人々を巻き込み、彼女ら／彼らの勝手な憶測が飛び交い、笑いあり、涙ありの人間が持つおかしみに触れるものでした。 藤岡は呉とメルボルンをめぐる戦後の歴史とその中を生きた女性の人生、さらには、かつて軍港として、そして戦後は臨海工業地帯として発展を遂げながらも、衰退してゆく地方都市である呉の現在に目を向けます。 そのような偶然と必然に翻弄されながらも逞しく生きた女性たちが辿った人生と彼女らが暮らした街を藤岡の視線から捉えることが本展の大きなテーマです。

写真とはとりかえしのつかないもの

これまでスナップを自身の作品の撮影技法とすることが多かった藤岡亜弥は、小型カメラにて自分が見たものを瞬間的に捉えることで、自分が見ていなかったものまで捉えてしまう不可逆性のことを「とりかえしのつかないもの」だと述べてきました。 本展の制作において、藤岡はある家庭で保管されていた写真たちに出会い、いわばファウンドフォトと言えるそれらを通じた作品制作に取り組みます。ファウンドフォトもスナップと同様に被写体の匿名性が共通しているのにもかかわらず、それが誰かというミステリがスナップよりも色濃く宙空に吊るされます。 誰かも分からない遥か過去の写真を通じて、赤の他人が出会い、交流を重ねてゆき、謎を解決しようとすればするほど、それはヒントにならず謎そのものになってゆく。撮影するばかりであった写真が解き明かすものへと変わるとき、「とりかえしのつかない」写真の意味もまた大きく変化してゆきます。

article_text:
S tand in any vaguely photogenic spot these days on holiday and the chances are you will come across people posing with raised phones and even ring lights. Some may be influencers with huge audiences on social media, others just overkeen Instagram users. With hotels and beauty spots now so overrun, however, bans on photography are coming into place.

The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, known for its glamorous clientele, views of the Côte d’Azur and a stunning infinity pool, has brought in rules against photoshoots: no longer allowed without prior permission.

According to reports , this has been prompted by people booking lunch reservations and bringing bags of clothing and jewellery. Instead of sitting down to eat, they have used their time at the hotel for photoshoots of themselves in different outfits, creating images to post to their social media accounts.

Less glamorous spots are also clamping down. The Hollies, a Cheshire farm shop which has become a popular content stop thanks to the Love Island star Molly-Mae Hague posting images from there, has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.

Meanwhile Jeremy King, the London restaurateur behind places such as Simpson’s in the Strand and the Park , wrote an article in the Evening Standard earlier this year titled: “I’m fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant – enough is enough.”

In the US, a shop on Nantucket, an island off Cape Cod, Massachusetts, went viral earlier this year for a sign reading “no influencers”, while the town of Pomfret in Vermont has banned influencers taking pictures in front of foliage in autumn. In Fujikawaguchiko in Japan , a screen has been put up near a convenience store to stop people taking pictures there in front of Mount Fuji.

Part of the argument from venues is that these photoshoots jeopardise privacy and discretion, especially as expected at expensive hotels. Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc’s manager, Sophie Volant, told Travel Weekly : “As much as [guests] appreciate having people in the restaurants and in the bars, they also want their summer home to remain private. We had to think about a solution.”

Anna Fedou, the chief marketing officer at the Beaumier hotel group, says it sometimes works with influencers to capture content to promote its luxury hotels, which include Les Roches Rouges near Marseille, loved for its photogenic pool. The group does not have specific rules around photography, Fedou says, but stays mindful of its primary purpose.

“We’re in the business of hospitality, not running photo studios,” she says. “People travel from all over the world to experience the atmosphere, sense of space and feeling that make a hotel unique. It’s our responsibility to protect that.”

Rules around photography at hotels and restaurants mirror a trend away from capturing the moment and towards being in it. Alex Goat, the founder of the youth culture agency Livity, compares these rules to clubs asking visitors to put stickers over their phones’ cameras. “They want to signify that they’re here for people who love music. There’s something potentially similar [here],” she says. “It’s ‘I’m here because I want to enjoy the space’ rather than ‘I’m here to document something to other people’.”

Part of the disapproval towards influencers is a common misconception is that they are paid well for such content. Sometimes, as with Beaumier hotels, influencers will produce posts in exchange for a free room, but the idea is that brands will want to make deals with influencers due to their association with glamorous locations. “The majority are creating most of their content for their audiences for free,” explains Nicole Ocran, an influencer who set up the Creator Union to represent those in the industry. “They create content in the hope of courting brands and seeing who will bite.”

There has been previous outrage around influencers’ behaviour, as in 2021 when Love Island stars travelled to Dubai during lockdown, for example. And if there is an underlying snobbery to a luxury hotel instigating anti-photoshoot policies, there may be sexism, too. “Influencer culture has always been vilified in popular culture,” says Sophie Bishop, the author of Influencer Creep . “It’s a very feminised form of media, that’s bound up in promotional culture.”

Ocran agrees. “Most people have a particular stereotype in mind,” she says. “That isn’t to say that influencers and content creators can’t overstep or be insufferable when getting their shots and filming in public.”

Fedou believes that the key is to walk a balance that engages with social media content while keeping a restful experience at hotels. “Influencers will generally choose quieter moments for shooting content, to capture the space without disturbing others,” she says. “Les Roches Rouges has a relaxed atmosphere, but guest experience always comes first.”

While the backlash might be aimed at influencers with lots of followers, over 5.4 billion people use social media every day .

Ocran hopes that rules around photography might promote a more balanced attitude to social media in general. “[It’s] pushing back against the idea that not every space is meant for public consumption, and not every experience should be turned into content,” she says. “And as a creator, that’s quite a healthy message to send to us all.”

article_text:
Paramount’s “ Street Fighter ” delivered a knockout blow to top the U.K. and Ireland box office, debuting in first place with £2.3 million ($3.1 million).

Universal’s animated feature “ Forgotten Island ” bowed in second position, taking $1.8 million in its opening session. TGS Cinemas Limited secured third place with the debut of Indian superstar Rajinikanth ‘s blockbuster “ Jailer 2 ,” collecting $1.6 million.

Sony’s psychological thriller “Verity” moved to fourth spot in its third frame, adding $1.5 million. The Colleen Hoover adaptation elevated its gross to $12.8 million. Universal’s supernatural horror “Other Mommy” followed in fifth place in its sophomore weekend, generating $1.3 million to push its cume to $5.1 million.

Trafalgar Releasing’s stage capture of “Hadestown: The Musical” debuted in sixth position with a weekend haul of $844,115, lifting its total box office to $2 million including earlier screenings. Disney’s’ survival thriller “Whalefall,” starring Austin Abrams and Josh Brolin, opened in seventh place, taking $691,000.

Paramount’s action thriller “Heart of the Beast,” starring Brad Pitt and J.K. Simmons, held eighth position in its fourth week, collecting $689,788 for a total of $8.6 million. Sony’s franchise reboot “Resident Evil” took ninth place in its fifth session, adding $653,396 to lift its cumulative total to $18.5 million. Universal’s “Sense and Sensibility” rounded out the top 10 in its fourth frame with $421,386, pushing its running cume to $7.9 million.

Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, mid-week debuts kick off on Wednesday with Zee Studios International rolling out Indian comedy sequel “Godday Godday Chaa 2,” Tull Stories releasing Scottish Ballet feature “These Violent Delights” directed by Christopher Hampson and Oscar Sansom, and Trafalgar Releasing presenting the stage production of Noel Coward’s “Fallen Angels”.

Wide commercial and saturation rollouts arriving on Friday 23 across 300+ locations are led by Warner Bros.’ DC horror thriller “Clayface”; Travis Knight’s stop-motion animated fantasy “Wildwood” via Black Bear, featuring the voices of Peyton Elizabeth Lee, Jacob Tremblay, Carey Mulligan, Mahershala Ali, and Angela Bassett; and Lionsgate U.K.’s comedy “Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.”

Releases also include Amazon MGM Studios’ comedy feature “Ali G: Who Iz I?”, Paramount’s animated family adventure “Tad and the Magic Lamp”, and 3000 Pictures’ sci-fi drama “Klara and the Sun”.

Specialized, festival, and international rollouts opening Friday include Moviegoers Entertainment’s Bollywood film “Udta Teer”; Mubi’s’s triple bill of “Junk,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s drama “Fatherland,” starring Sandra Hüller and Hanns Zischler across 25+ locations, and Eleanor Coppola’s documentary “Making Marie Antoinette,” featuring Sofia Coppola and Kirsten Dunst across 25+ screens; Netflix’s “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong and starring Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, and Zo In-sung across 25+ sites; Glimmerama’s documentary “All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea,” directed by Jeanie Finlay; Exposure’s “Children of the Wicker Man”; Kazoo Films’ animated title “Monster Mia”; and “Bad Day At.”

Repertory screenings are anchored by Park Circus launching the 30th anniversary 4K restoration of Wes Craven’s “Scream,” starring Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox, and David Arquette, across 100+ screens.

The weekend wraps with extensive event cinema and concert programming, beginning on Friday with “Blood Saga.” Saturday features Disney’s “Disney Junior Cinema Club 2026” alongside Trafalgar Releasing’s event broadcasts of “HYBE Cheering Party”, Seventeen’s world tour “NEW_”, and Tomorrow X Together’s world tour “Act : Tomorrow”. The frame concludes on Sunday with Trafalgar Releasing’s one-night-only live viewing of “BTS World Tour ‘Arirang’ in Buenos Aires,” directed by Jungjae Ha, across 300+ locations.

"对丹妮尔而言，绘画是唤醒这种原始力量的一种方式。为了启动她的精神天线，她一笔接一笔地勾勒。在她的画笔下，浮现出一个跪在火盆旁祈祷的女人。在一层面纱的褶皱之间，显现出一个消失的新娘的面容。在另一张纸上，一个身体被串在天空中。一根沙爹竹签穿透下巴，又从头顶穿出。这里有影子生物、镜面传送门、念珠和枝叶繁茂的森林景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对丹妮尔来说，没有任何事物是孤立存在的。在手部的运动中，她在纸上寻找着各种连接。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这根辫子的第二股代表了大地。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在她的一幅画作中，丹妮尔将自己描绘在花茎和稀疏的树冠之间。她弓起脊背，双手伸向地面。回到大地（Back to Earth）。植物、动物和人类一次又一次地被并排描绘，不分高下。大自然是诱人的，但天堂之中也潜伏着危险。蛇在植被间盘旋。鳄鱼露出了牙齿。它们是奇美绝伦的生物，却又同时致命。丹妮尔并没有消除这些对立，而是让它们并存。美丽与威胁。人性与兽性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/3.-Back-to-Earth-Acryl-en-conte-op-papier-115-x-75-cm.-2022-1118x1600.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "丹妮尔·勒迈尔（Danielle Lemaire）——回到大地（Back to Earth），丙烯和康特蜡笔纸本，115 x 75 cm，2022年。", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些画作中隐藏着一种对自然的另一种视角：自然不是某种与人类分离、我们可以掌控或驯服的事物，而是我们自身所是其一部分的事物。蛇也活在我们体内。鳄鱼可以像一位老朋友一样被拥抱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这根辫子的第三股也是最后一股代表了丹妮尔的先祖，从而与印度尼西亚及其历史相连。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在年轻时从爪哇搬到荷兰的父亲去世后，丹妮尔深入研究了自己的家族过去和印尼根源。她收集照片和书籍，建立个人档案，并了解各种神话与仪式。但过去无法被完全重建。材料中缺少了面容和名字。许多故事在时间的流逝中失落了，或被暴力抹去了。印度尼西亚的历史、她先祖的过去，由于殖民视角的凝视而失去了焦点。通过将殖民时期的档案材料与个人符号和联想交织在一起，丹妮尔试图重新对焦这一影像。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/4.-Het-Meisje-en-de-Krokodil-Acryl-en-conte-op-papier-30-x-21-cm-2025-1184x1600.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "丹妮尔·勒迈尔（Danielle Lemaire）——女孩与鳄鱼（Het Meisje en de Krokodil），丙烯和康特蜡笔纸本，30 x 21 cm，2025年。", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她的先祖在她耳边低语，诉说那些长期以来不为人知的事物：韧性、社群，以及那些声音未被听见的人们（多为女性）的生活。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着第三股的加入，这根辫子便完整了。从那一刻起，很难再分清哪一股到哪里结束、哪一股从哪里开始。这些主题相互流淌、穿梭并交织在彼此下方。宇宙、大地、先祖，共同融为一体。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.mistermotley.nl/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/5.-Gadis-Cermin-Spiegelmeisjes-Mixed-media-58-x-225-cm-2026-1.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "丹妮尔·勒迈尔（Danielle Lemaire）——Gadis Cermin（镜面女孩），综合媒介，58 x 22,5 cm，2026年。", "credit": "Mister Motley", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "—", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在海伦芬（Heereveen）的盖泰肯特画廊（Galerie Getekend），丹妮尔·勒迈尔（Danielle Lemaire）的个展《Origin》将一直展出至2026年11月8日。2027年，迪彭海姆绘画中心（Drawing Centre Diepenheim）将举办她的作品个展。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Noa Zuidervaart pluist Danielle Lemaire’s werk uit ware het een vlecht. ‘Danielle ziet haren als geleiders, als ‘spirituele antennes’ die ons afstemmen op wat zich onder of achter de zichtbare werkelijkheid bevindt. In haar tekeningen zijn figuren vaak herkenbaar aan hun haardracht. Hoe het haar valt, wordt samengebonden, het gezicht verhult of wild langs het lichaam golft: het onthult een innerlijke wereld die we doorgaans via de blik of het gelaat proberen te doorgronden. Dat juist het haar die rol vervult, is geen toeval. Over de hele wereld, in tal van culturen, wordt er een bijzondere oerkracht aan toegeschreven. Haar draagt energie, belichaamt levenskracht en verbindt ons met de wereld om ons heen.’

Facebook

X

Linkedin

Link kopiëren

Een klassieke haarvlecht ontstaat uit drie gelijke strengen. Scheid de strengen bij de kruin van het hoofd en kruis daarna steeds een van de buitenste strengen over de middelste. Herhaal deze beweging: Links over het midden, rechts over het midden, links over het midden, rechts over het midden. Steeds opnieuw.

Wanneer je het werk van kunstenaar Danielle Lemaire als een vlecht beschouwt, als een metafoor om haar werk te duiden, kun je ook daarin drie strengen onderscheiden. Drie thema’s die steeds terugkeren. Net als de haren in een vlecht, zijn ze verweven. Om te herleiden hoe de vlecht is ontstaan, ontrafel je haar streng voor streng, helemaal terug tot aan de wortels.

De eerste streng van deze vlecht representeert de kosmos.

Danielle ziet haren als geleiders, als ‘spirituele antennes’ die ons afstemmen op wat zich onder of achter de zichtbare werkelijkheid bevindt. In haar tekeningen zijn figuren vaak herkenbaar aan hun haardracht. Hoe het haar valt, wordt samengebonden, het gezicht verhult of wild langs het lichaam golft: het onthult een innerlijke wereld die we doorgaans via de blik of het gelaat proberen te doorgronden. Dat juist het haar die rol vervult, is geen toeval. Over de hele wereld, in tal van culturen, wordt er een bijzondere oerkracht aan toegeschreven. Haar draagt energie, belichaamt levenskracht en verbindt ons met de wereld om ons heen.

Tekenen is voor Danielle een manier om die oerkracht op te roepen. Om haar spirituele antennes aan te zetten, trekt ze lijn na lijn. Vanuit haar potlood ontstaat een vrouw, knielend en biddend naast een vuurschaal. Tussen de plooien van een sluier verschijnt het gezicht van een verdwenen bruid. Op een ander blad wordt een lichaam aan de hemel geregen. Een satéprikker doorboort de kin en komt vanuit de kruin weer tevoorschijn. Er zijn schaduwwezens, spiegelportalen, rozenkransen en dichtbegroeide boslandschappen.

Voor Danielle staat niets op zichzelf. In de beweging van haar hand zoekt ze de connecties op papier.

De tweede streng van deze vlecht representeert de aarde.

In een van haar tekeningen heeft Danielle zichzelf afgebeeld tussen bloemstengels en een ijl bladerdek. Ze buigt haar rug voorover en reikt met haar handen naar de grond. Back to Earth. Terug naar de aarde. Steeds opnieuw worden plant, dier en mens naast elkaar afgebeeld, zonder hiërarchie. De natuur is verleidelijk, maar ook in het paradijs ligt gevaar op de loer. Tussen de begroeiing kronkelen slangen. Krokodillen laten er hun tanden zien. Wonderbaarlijk mooie wezens, maar tegelijk levensgevaarlijk. Danielle heft die tegenstellingen niet op, maar laat ze naast elkaar bestaan. De schoonheid en de dreiging. Het menselijke en het dierlijke.

In de tekeningen schuilt een ander perspectief op de natuur: niet als iets dat losstaat van de mens, iets wat we kunnen beheersen of temmen, maar als iets waar we zelf onderdeel van zijn. De slang leeft ook in ons. De krokodil mag als een goede vriend omarmd worden.

De derde en laatste streng van deze vlecht representeert Danielle’s voorouders, en is daarmee verbonden met Indonesië en haar geschiedenis.

Na het overlijden van haar vader, die als jongeman van Java naar Nederland verhuist, verdiept Danielle zich in haar familieverleden en Indonesische wortels. Ze verzamelt foto’s en boeken, legt een persoonlijk archief aan en leert over mythen en rituelen. Maar het verleden laat zich niet volledig reconstrueren. In het materiaal ontbreken gezichten en namen. Veel verhalen zijn door de tijd verloren gegaan of met geweld uitgewist. De geschiedenis van Indonesië, het verleden van haar voorouders, is door een koloniale blik uit focus geraakt. Door archiefmateriaal uit de koloniale periode te vermengen met persoonlijke symbolen en associaties, probeert Danielle het beeld opnieuw scherp te stellen.

Haar voorouders fluisteren in haar oor over wat lang onzichtbaar was: veerkracht, gemeenschap en de levens van mensen, meestal vrouwen, die ongehoord zijn gebleven.

Met de derde streng is de vlecht compleet. Vanaf dat moment is het moeilijk om nog te achterhalen waar de ene streng ophoudt en de andere begint. De thema’s lopen over, door en onder elkaar heen. Kosmos, aarde, voorouders, samen één geheel.

—

In Galerie Getekend in Heereveen is nog tot 8 november 2026 en met Danielle Lemaire’s solotentoonstelling Origin te zien. In 2027 presenteert Drawing Centre Diepenheim een solotentoonstelling van haar werk.

Il progetto riunirà lavori realizzati con tecniche e supporti differenti – olio, pastello, grafite, serigrafia, acrilico – per restituire una ricerca di ampio respiro, sviluppata a partire dal lettering e progressivamente spinta verso una dimensione più astratta, nella quale la parola perde la propria funzione semantica per diventare forma, ritmo, superficie e tensione visiva. La scomposizione della parola scritta è rimasta un elemento ricorrente. Le lettere, ereditate dalla cultura del writing, vengono private della loro immediata leggibilità e trasformate in strutture geometriche, segni calligrafici e campiture. article_text:
Aprirà il 21 novembre 2026 negli spazi di SPAZIOC21 a Reggio Emilia The machine won’t understand , mostra personale di Zero-T , al secolo Paolo Capezzuoli , artista attivo da oltre tre decenni tra writing, graphic design, cultura hip hop e streetwear. Il progetto riunirà lavori realizzati con tecniche e supporti differenti – olio, pastello, grafite, serigrafia, acrilico – per restituire una ricerca di ampio respiro, sviluppata a partire dal lettering e progressivamente spinta verso una dimensione più astratta, nella quale la parola perde la propria funzione semantica per diventare forma, ritmo, superficie e tensione visiva. Ad accompagnare la mostra sarà anche un libro d’artista con un contributo critico di Carlo McCormick , storico dell’arte e curatore legato alla scena underground newyorkese.

Fin dal titolo, The machine won’t understand introduce uno dei temi centrali della mostra: il rapporto tra gesto umano e tecnologia. Il punto di partenza non è una contrapposizione frontale tra analogico e digitale, quanto piuttosto l’attenzione per ciò che è difficilmente codificabile, ovvero l’imprevisto, l’errore, l’intuizione, l’irregolarità del gesto e la componente fisica del processo creativo.

Tra lettering e superficie

La pratica di Zero-T affonda le proprie radici nel graffiti writing ma nel tempo ha progressivamente ampliato il proprio campo d’azione, attraversando pittura, design, grafica, tessile e prodotto industriale. La scomposizione della parola scritta è rimasta un elemento ricorrente. Le lettere, ereditate dalla cultura del writing, vengono private della loro immediata leggibilità e trasformate in strutture geometriche, segni calligrafici e campiture. La tipografia smette così di funzionare come veicolo di un messaggio esplicito e diventa materia visiva.

La superficie mantiene però una memoria della strada, sovrapposizioni, stratificazioni, contorni marcati e interferenze tra tecniche diverse conservano qualcosa dell’instabilità e della provvisorietà del muro urbano, anche quando il lavoro viene trasferito nello spazio espositivo.

L’imperfezione come metodo

Un altro nucleo della mostra riguarda il colore, utilizzato senza una grammatica rigidamente prefissata. Contrasti, accostamenti inattesi e slittamenti cromatici vengono lasciati entrare nel processo come elementi creativi. È in questo senso che il titolo della mostra assume una funzione programmatica: The machine won’t understand rivendica la componente non completamente prevedibile del fare artistico e la possibilità che un lavoro prenda forma anche attraverso deviazioni, accidenti e decisioni intuitive.

Il riferimento alla macchina non riguarda quindi soltanto l’intelligenza artificiale o le tecnologie digitali contemporanee ma più in generale ogni sistema fondato sulla ripetibilità e sulla codificazione. A questo modello Zero-T contrappone una pratica che mantiene aperto il margine dell’instabilità.

Zero-T, dalla cultura hip hop allo streetwear

La traiettoria di Paolo Capezzuoli prende avvio a metà degli anni Ottanta, quando insieme a Nicola “ Deemo-Dayaki ” fonda la crew CMC – Color Melodies Combo. Durante i soggiorni a New York entra in contatto con realtà centrali della cultura hip hop e del writing, tra cui Rock Steady Crew e TDS – The Death Squad. Parallelamente sviluppa una ricerca nel campo della grafica e dell’abbigliamento, contribuendo alla diffusione in Italia di un immaginario legato alla street culture.

Nel 1989 inizia il rapporto con Slam Jam , fondata da Luca Benini , per la quale realizza il primo logo e successivamente progetti grafici, capsule collection e collaborazioni. Il suo lavoro si estende così anche al rapporto tra arti visive, moda e costruzione dell’identità di brand legati allo streetwear. Zero-T opera in questo contesto attraverso la definizione di concept, sistemi visivi e linguaggi che mettono in comunicazione grafica, abbigliamento e cultura urbana.

Nel 2014 Zero-T presenta la sua prima personale alla galleria 1 Opera di Napoli. L’anno successivo partecipa a The Bridges of Graffiti , progetto presentato durante la 56ma Biennale di Venezia, insieme ad artisti come Futura2000, Todd James, Doze Green, Skki, JayOne, Eron e Mode2 .

article_text:
Costume designer Grace Snell had never done a period film before she jumped on a call with filmmaker Georgia Oakley . You can approach historical costumes in many ways, but Snell wanted to tackle the project with both good sense (in-depth research into Regency England) and a particularly modern sensibility .

“ I often think about when I look at the ‘Little Women’ that was made in the ’40s, and the ‘Little Women’ that was made in the ’90s, and the ‘Little Women’ that was made a few years ago. Although you are designing for period, even in the 1940s version of ‘Little Women,’ you can see 1940s fashions,” Snell told IndieWire. “ I love the idea of making something that feels that it is of the time now, and of where we are, particularly as women: how we’re dressing and what we see in our friends.”

So the 2026 “Sense and Sensibility” would of course feature the gracious dresses with empire waists and jaunty ribbons and frock coats that pop up in nearly all adaptations of Austen’s first novel, charting the adventures of the pragmatic-to-a-fault Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and romantic Marianne ( Esmé Creed-Miles ). But Snell was just as inspired by the fashion of the ‘90s and early ‘00s — which do feature a similar silhouette to Austen’s own era — and by the relationship families and friends have to clothes that are timeless.

Namely, that sisters are in and out of each other’s closets.

Snell wanted the Dashwoods to dress as if no whole costume team is coordinating things behind them — though haughty sister-in-law Fanny (Stacy Martin) is another matter. Especially once they’re pushed out of their family home and must make do in a cottage in Devonshire, Snell wanted to show how the girls borrow from each other, adapt odds and ends, and don’t always put outfits together to match. By the end of the film, Snell wanted what the two heroines have learned from each other to reflect in how they dress.

But Elinor and Marianne start out with distinct philosophies that Snell brought to the first costume fittings. “You could tell how Daisy was Elinor and how Esme was Marianne instantly, even in how I set up the fitting for them. Daisy was very structured, very formulaic, labeled; it was systematic in how we tried on things. And then with Esmé, I bought loads of fun things, boxes of trims and ribbons and flouncy things, a lot of hats, and it was about accessorizing and playing,” Snell said. “I got her to dress herself, and I wanted to see how she might make ‘mistakes’ dressing herself, how things might not be done up correctly.”

Marianne, after all, isn’t really concerned with correctness or propriety (to Elinor’s continual dismay), so Snell and Creed-Miles embraced those instinctual first choices in crafting a look for Marianne that was just a bit irreverent and rebellious. Snell decided the character would reach back to “vintage” fashion from older eras, keep dresses she loved that were a bit too big and adapt them, and sport a sash around her waist — being the dashing cavalry officer she wants to see in the world.

Marianne feels most vulnerable and out of place in a “correct” ballgown in London, heartsick for the handsome Willoughby (Frank Dillane) and without allies when she sees him again. “ I really wanted to show how intimidating a place like London could be when you don’t have the means, through what everyone’s wearing at the ball,” Snell said.

The sisters are much more at ease in Barton, needless to say, and Snell found sneaky ways to show how they adapt and learn from each other. She gave both Elinor and Marianne jackets cut from the same pattern, but crafted to express their different sensibilities.

“We lengthened Elinor’s to make it a longer jacket, which is something that was used in the time [period], and then they were made in different fabrics but the same color. They could wear the same outfit, but they were styled differently. So [the characters] are in those details,” Snell said. “This is about pulling down the pedestal of what Period Drama is and seeing ourselves in these characters contextually with clothing.”

More than any of the Dashwoods, no one embodies that unabashed joy of expressing oneself through clothes like the voluble Mrs. Jennings (Fiona Shaw). Snell wanted to challenge the audience’s perceptions of how women of a certain age dress by giving Mrs. Jennings a style as excitable as she is. “I think she’s a romantic at heart and is very conscious of what she looks like and what she wears and tries things that don’t necessarily fit some of the societal expectations for an older woman,” Snell said. “But I imagined that she just wears things she likes the look of, and I had a lot of fun with Fiona.”

It was fun for Shaw, as well, who’d never gotten the Regency costume treatment before. “Fiona would always, you know, get dressed with me and just be like, ‘What are we wearing today? This is just such a wild ride,’” Snell said.

It’s a wild ride for every character, from Mrs. Dashwood’s slightly too-gracious gowns (Catríona Balfe) to the utter betrayal of Willoughby’s glittering vest in London (based on a CosProp archive piece that uses a natural material called cellulose for its sequins). But that’s because Snell leaned into letting the characters in “Sense and Sensibility” dress the way we always do: expressing ourselves by picking things from the people around us.

“Sense and Sensibility” is now in theaters.

Borden）1983年的《烈火中生》（Born in Flames）打了大制作激素，再加冰镇伺候——随后它展开了一场场精心编排的动作戏，最初由激进的移民防卫活动家佩菲迪亚·贝弗利希尔斯（Perfidia Beverly Hills，由多栖艺人特亚纳·泰勒饰）组织。一次失败的银行抢劫，连同一辆在拥堵车流中穿行的逃跑汽车，构成了这位身怀六甲的革命者被捕及其最终失踪的前奏。", article_text:
Crashing into the zeitgeist against who-knows-what headwinds, Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another is just one dang thing after another, not to mention an impressive addition to the imposing edifice of the Anderson oeuvre. After an assertive if choppy start as a kick-ass, madcap, somewhat kinky, antifascist quasi–superhero flick—imagine Lizzie Borden’s Born in Flames (1983) on big-budget steroids, served over ICE—it unfurls choreographed action sequences, initially organized by the militant immigrant-defense activist Perfidia Beverly Hills (multi-hyphenate Teyana Taylor). A failed bank job, complete with getaway car threading through gridlocked traffic, provides the prelude to the pregnant revolutionary’s bust and eventual disappearance.

Jumping ahead 16 years (from when to when is never explicitly stated), the movie settles briefly into cannabis-infused slapstick to find Perfidia’s ex, the washed-up militant Bob Ferguson (Leonardo DiCaprio), living below the radar in redwood-forest exile with the couple’s feisty adolescent daughter, Willa (Chase Infiniti). Their quiet life (a rondo of sitcom banter, with a suitably absurd parent-teacher conference in which Bob checks the political correctness of the school’s lesson plans) is disrupted when an intervention by the family’s implacable nemesis, Col. Steven J. Lockjaw (Sean Penn), triggers the extended chase sequence that consumes the rest of the film. Bob is just firing up a doobie to dig The Battle of Algiers (1966) in brain-addled splendor when Lockjaw’s SWAT team descends from the heavens for another battle—busting up Willa’s queer-friendly high-school dance, terrorizing the town’s Latino workers, and creating mayhem that, escalating for nearly two hours, has Bob pursued throughout California, still in his flannel bathrobe.

Anderson is an admirer of Thomas Pynchon. Having successfully adapted the writer’s hippie noir Inherent Vice in 2014, he credits Pynchon’s Vineland (something like Inherent Vice ’s anticipatory sequel) with inspiring One Battle . Published in 1990 and set at the height of the Reagan reaction in 1984, Vineland evokes the passing of the counterculture—with even greater richness, it mines the same territory as Sidney Lumet’s Running on Empty (1988), as well as John Sayles’s Return of the Secaucus 7 (1979) and its wretched rip-off The Big Chill (1983).

Instead of adapting the novel, Anderson essentially borrows Vineland ’s basic situation: a burned-out counterculture radical hides out in rural California with his teenage daughter. The girl’s mother, a revolutionary firebrand, has long since disappeared; father and daughter are threatened by the reappearance of a government agent with whom they tangled in the past. The attitude is Pynchonesque as well: like Anderson’s Inherent Vice , One Battle has a cartoony quality evident in the performances as well as the character names.

Pumped up and rigid, with facial contortions suggesting a hot poker up his butt, Penn’s Lockjaw is the actor’s most outlandish physical performance since he played high-school stoner Jeff Spicoli in 1982’s Fast Times at Ridgemont High (to name-check another Reagan-era movie). As the proprietor of the local Ninja Academy, Benicio Del Toro’s Sergio St. Carlos coolly navigates the carnage, stealing every scene with pursed lips and a drolly arched eyebrow. (As a comic team, DiCaprio and Del Toro rival Del Toro and Johnny Depp in Terry Gilliam’s Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas .) The fruit of revolutionary love, Sergio’s student Willa (sarcastically and erroneously identified by one of Lockjaw’s minions as “the only high-school girl in America that doesn’t have a phone”) is a fully convincing neophyte martial artist. (Infiti herself is a trained kickboxer.)

One Battle is not only tumultuous but funny. Anderson can’t resist satirizing woke jargon and underground protocols. Bob’s prolonged telephonic struggle with his underground contact “Comrade Josh” over his quasi-dormant revolutionary cell’s “greeting code” is the movie’s most sustained running gag. It’s also splendidly self-referential. Chased by highway patrol, Sergio needs to propel Bob out of a speeding car: “No fear, like Tom Fucking Cruise!” (Did DiCaprio do his own stunts? No matter.) Bob bails, hot-wires another automobile, and drives off over crazy highway hills in search of the abducted Willa. Ultimately, and quite movingly, One Battle is a story of father and daughter. Not for nothing does Tom Petty’s heartbreaking “American Girl” (along with Gil Scott-Heron’s “The Revolution Will Not Be Televised”) play over the end credits. Venceremos .

Speaking of love stories, I confess that I didn’t get Licorice Pizza (2021)—has there ever been a less appetizing title?—and am in no great rush to see it again. Still, that movie’s most impressive scene—Alana Haim piloting a monster moving truck—now seems like a dry run for One Battle ’s orchestrated car chases. This is very much an action film. Anderson may not care much for genres, Inherent Vice being an exception, but he always seems to have formidable filmmakers and their films in mind. Thus, Boogie Nights matched itself against Scorsese’s Goodfellas and Magnolia seemingly addressed Altman’s Short Cuts . The go-for-baroque There Will Be Blood took on Welles and the studied perfection of The Master evoked Kubrick. If Phantom Thread could be seen as a rewriting of ’40s Hitchcock, One Battle After Another appears to engage something closer to home, namely Quentin Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood . The title has a Tarantino-esque mano-a-mano ring even as it reinforces the movie’s split temporal structure—though unlike in Once Upon a Time… , here both battles suggest the ’60s without actually being set in the ’60s.

One of the few working Hollywood directors who might qualify for a degree in American Studies, Anderson has made some impressively heady period films. Boogie Nights revived the hung-over ’70s; adapted from Upton Sinclair, There Will Be Blood pondered unfettered frontier capitalism and manifest destiny; The Master evoked the post–World War II “American Century.” One Battle , however, is aggressively present-tense—if anything, it seems to be set, like the adventures of A.I. TV host Max Headroom, 20 minutes into the future. I saw the movie only days after a youthful assassin elevated right-wing agitator Charlie Kirk to Horst Wessel martyrdom, and the same morning that the Trump regime, whose followers are parodied in the movie as the extralegal white-supremacist Christmas Adventurers Club, threatened a crackdown on an imagined network of left-wing terrorists. Variety reported the movie’s price tag at $175 million, and Warner Bros., which admits to $130 million, has got to be wondering if said crackdown will be good, bad, or very bad for business. I can’t speak to that, but I can testify that Anderson’s Battle is good for cinema. This rambunctious (hey guys, it’s only a) movie is not just energetic, but energizing.

article_text:
PHOTOBOOK DESIGN WITH ANN GRIFFIN

Dates: 07-10.03.2024, 10:00 – 17:00 daily

Venue: Matca Space for Photography, 48 Ngoc Ha, Ba Dinh, Hanoi

Language: English

Tuition fee: 5,000,000 VND

Limited to 8 participants

Register before 24.02 via Google Form

The photobook design workshop invites photographers and designers interested in the bookmaking process. Led by experienced Swiss designer Ann Griffin and conducted in English, the workshop includes both theoretical inputs and hands-on exercises. Participants should work towards finishing a ready-to-print book dummy over the course of 4 days. The workshop is limited to a small group of 8 participants, allowing for active engagement and personalized feedback.

A long-standing format for presenting photographic works, the photobook is a contemporary phenomenon globally. Yet contrary to popular belief, photography and photobooks in particular are hardly a universal medium. Rather, they are directly informed by the history, culture, and even the socio-political environment of the locale. This workshop thus offers the space for mutual learning where we share industry experiences, take inspiration from diverse publications produced across different times and places, and discuss opportunities and challenges for publishing in the context of Vietnam.

The workshop is organized by Matca and supported by the Swiss Arts Council Pro Helvetia.

Workshop content

• Individual and group feedback about the photography project and book concept • Editing images, preparing layouts, brainstorming cover ideas • Thinking about the book as an object (printing techniques, materials, sizes, feelings, etc.) • Producing the dummy file • Sharing about the book-making process • Sharing about publishers, distributors & self-publishing examples in Switzerland and Europe, plus Vietnam and Southeast Asia.

A detailed agenda will be sent to selected participants prior to the workshop.

Eligibility & registration

The workshop is open to photographers and designers interested in learning about the bookmaking process.

Participants who are photographers should have a photography project ready to be edited with the intention of making a publication. Participants who are designers should find a photography project they would like to turn into a publication, preferably one that is complete but has yet to be published. All genres of photography are welcome.

Participants should prepare a wide edit of 50 – 100 images from one project in digital files and small 9×12 prints. They should have a good command of English and a personal laptop with Adobe CC or similar software. All participants are expected to commit to the full program and finish a book dummy at the end of the workshop.

About the instructor

Ann Griffin (1981) is a graphic designer specializing in editorial design. She has a Bachelor’s Degree in Visual Communication from HEAD—Geneva in 2007 and a Master’s in Editorial Design in 2022 from Elisava, Barcelona. In 2010, she co-founded Studio-Rubic in Geneva, a graphic design practice that worked for various clients and publishers until 2018. Based in Zürich, she now collaborates with publishers, photographers and artists on different book projects, with a particular interest in photography books.

Ann has worked with Edition Patrick Frey, Aperture New York, Fonds d’art Contemporain Genève, Bec en l’Air, Piano Nobile, Edition Notari, Metis Presses, Vexer Verlag (upcoming) as well as numerous artists and photographers on self-published publications. Since 2017, she has been part of the committee of near. (Swiss Association for Contemporary Photography), where she has been organizing events and co-managing the association.

article_text:
Toni Collette will make her feature directing debut with “The Best Of,” her screen version of Graeme Simsion’s bestselling novel, which is one of 75 projects sharing more than AUD16.9 million ($11.7 million) in production and development money from Screen Australia .

Collette, an Emmy and Golden Globe winner, produces alongside Christopher Simon. The story centers on two ex-lovers who come back into each other’s lives after spending decades apart, only to find old feelings stirring with messy and mixed results. Screen Australia made a major production investment in association with Screen NSW. Kismet handles local distribution and Cornerstone holds international sales.

Related Stories

Michaela Jaé Rodriguez to Receive APLA Health’s Voice of Visibility Award at AIDS Walk Los Angeles (EXCLUSIVE)

Atlanta Hawks Strike Streaming Alliance With Amazon's Prime Video

The round, announced Tuesday, covers features, series and shorts.

“Australian storytellers continue to captivate audiences with their creativity, originality and distinctive perspectives. This latest round of funding supports an exciting range of projects from emerging creatives forging new paths to established voices exploring new creative territory. Screen Currency 2026 found that local stories matter deeply to Australians, and these projects will deliver on the authenticity and ambition that audiences have come to expect,” said Louise Gough, Screen Australia’s director of narrative content.

Brouhaha Entertainment, the company behind “Boy Swallows Universe,” is making “The Dark Lake,” a series based on Sarah Bailey’s award-winning novel. Tonkin plays a detective in a rural town whose investigation into the killing of a former high school classmate forces her to face buried secrets of her own. Troy Lum and Andrew Mason produce, with Becca Johnstone writing and executive producing. Giorgia Stawaruk, Tonkin and Katarina Mandic are also executive producers. Screenwest partners on the major production investment, with additional financing from Screen NSW.

Jeffrey Walker (“The Artful Dodger,” “Fing!”) directs “Bull” (working title), a feature from Infin8 Studios and Total Fiction Films. Drawn from a true story, it follows a smooth-talking prisoner who signs up for a debating team inside Tasmania’s harshest jail, hoping to change course and finally give his mother a reason to be proud. George Pullar stars, co-writes with Taylor Danworth and produces with Michael Lawrence, John Molloy and Suzanne Walker. Richard Roxburgh, Robyn Malcolm, Teresa Palmer, Thomas M Wright and Harrison Gilbertson round out the cast. Screen Queensland is on board, with Kismet distributing locally and Cornerstone handling international sales.

Sooshi Mango’s untitled feature debut follows three obstinate Italian immigrants who mobilize their multicultural neighborhood when a mysterious wellness club puts their cherished social club at risk. Nick Kozakis (“Kick On”) directs from a script by the group’s Joe Salanitri, Carlo Salanitri and Andrew Manfre with Declan Fay. Paul Dainty and Cathy Rodda produce, with Timothy Whiting as co-producer. VicScreen partners, and Roadshow has local distribution.

Rodd Rathjen directs “No Friend But the Mountains,” adapted from Behrouz Boochani’s acclaimed memoir, from a screenplay he co-wrote with Boochani. The Kurdish journalist, fleeing persecution, is intercepted at sea and sent to Manus Island, where he documents the gradual breakdown of the men held there. Gal Greenspan, Sharlene George, Amy Parry, Arkos Armont, Katy Roberts, Boochani and Antony Waddington produce. The New Zealand Film Commission, Screen Queensland and VicScreen are partners, with Madman distributing in Australia.

On the development side, Mithila Gupta’s “Desi Down Under” will turn her coming-of-age Indian-Australian audio series into a romantic comedy feature about three misfits who head from Kerala to the beach at Coogee, where they hope to pick up surf-lifesaving skills they can use to help their compatriots. Gupta writes and produces with Nina Aujla, Smriti Mundhra and Maya Gnyp.

Goalpost Pictures’ series “The Caretaker,” adapted from Gabriel Bergmoser’s bestselling novel by Alexei Mizin and Ryan van Dijk, both members of Screen Australia’s 2026 Talent Gateway cohort, also landed development backing. The thriller centers on a woman hiding out as caretaker of a ski resort out of season, who goes to ever more extreme lengths to hold on to the life she has built.

Among the shorts, BAFTA-nominated Rosie Westhoff (“The Main Part”) writes and directs “Solastalgia,” in which a young girl tries to reassemble scattered memories of the bushfire that destroyed her home while looking for connection in a transformed place. Chloe Brennan (“We Used to Own Houses”), Amanda Browne and Ashlee Russell (both “Mothmama”) produce, with Kitty Green (“The Royal Hotel”) as mentor.

Green also mentors the team behind a family short from Pasifika-led Mana Film Productions that mixes live action and animation, “My Life as a 12-Year-Old Demon Hunter… With Great Hair!” It tracks 12-year-old Tala over a single day as she fends off demons out to steal her powers – a bigger headache than her homework. AWGIE winner and bestselling author Maria Lewis writes, directs and co-produces, with Shonee Samia co-producing and Herbert Leota animating. Animator Jake Duczynski (“Magic Beach”) joins Green as mentor. Both shorts received principal production funding.

Full lists of production, development and short film approvals are on Screen Australia’s website. The agency will reveal more recently funded projects alongside the ABC Media Showcase on Oct. 21.

editorial_title_zh: 瑞士摄影基金会启动大型项目“保持运动中的保存”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 瑞士摄影基金会启动了迄今为止最大规模的开发项目：到2031年，它将对大约160个档案进行保护性保存、数字化并向公众开放。这一历时五年的大型项目构成了……的核心战略…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "瑞士摄影基金会启动了迄今为止最大规模的开发项目：到2031年，它将对大约160个档案进行保护性保存、数字化并向公众开放。这一历时五年的大型项目构成了该基金会战略重新定位的核心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该项目的中心是大约160个档案的物理和内容处理，这些档案由摄影基金会代表联邦管理，总共包含估计350万件藏品。每个档案的内部秩序都将被确定并可视化，摄影作品将被记录并在内容上进行描述，重新打包到适合档案的材料中，并通过安全数字化选择部分以便为未来保存。与此同时，还将对仓库进行现代化改造并扩建数字基础设施。在接下来的五年里，将分别有三个团队同时在一个档案上工作，并得到来自保护、数据库管理、数字化和物流方面的专业专家的支持。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "除了对复古照片、接触印片、幻灯片和底片进行物理保存之外（这些材料需要根据不同的材料进行不同的处理和储存），保护数量众多且部分面临严重威胁的底片藏品也十分紧迫：特别是1970年之前曝光的电影胶片材料通常由硝酸纤维素或醋酸盐组成，尽管其降解可以通过恒温恒湿储存来减慢，但无法阻止。摄影基金会通过复制摄影将其次数数字化；主文件保存在数字长期档案中，图像通过“在线图片档案”向公众开放。来自混合档案的日益增加的数字图像藏品带来了新的挑战。项目团队正在应对这些挑战。从长远来看，可靠的藏品数据应做到机器可读、标准化并通过永久链接持久访问，从而确保能够与其它科学数据进行互联。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在格吕岑大街45号的门厅现场，访客将持续获悉项目进展情况。小酒馆和图书馆保持开放。从2027年6月起，首个工场展览将展示该基金会的重要收藏领域。数字传播将得到加强。录制的口述历史访谈丰富了每月的“开箱”（Out of the Box）工场活动以及每年举行三次的“未来档案”（Archives For Future），后者是一系列关于已完成档案的讲座和对话。由于温特图尔的大型展览空间在未来几年内将用于档案工作，摄影基金会从2027年起将更多地在外部（extra muros）开展展览活动。与巴塞尔艺术博物馆、奥尔滕历史博物馆、帕斯夸尔摄影论坛和图尔高艺术博物馆的合作已经敲定。因此，摄影基金会在2027年及随后的几年里将在全瑞士范围内吸引越来越多的观众。", "translated": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Die Fotostiftung Schweiz startet ihr bislang grösstes Erschliessungsprojekt: Bis 2031 wird sie rund 160 Archive konservatorisch sichern, digitalisieren und der Öffentlichkeit zugänglich machen. Das auf fünf Jahre angelegte Grossprojekt bildet den Kern der strategischen Neuausrichtung der Stiftung."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Im Zentrum des Projekts steht die physische und inhaltliche Aufarbeitung der rund 160 Archive, welche die Fotostiftung im Auftrag des Bundes betreut und die zusammen geschätzt 3,5 Millionen Objekte umfassen. Für jedes Archiv wird die innere Ordnung festgestellt und sichtbar gemacht, die Fotografien werden erfasst und inhaltlich beschrieben, in archivtaugliche Materialien umgepackt und eine Auswahl durch Sicherungsdigitalisierungen für die Zukunft bewahrt. Parallel dazu erfolgen die Modernisierung der Depots und der Ausbau der digitalen Infrastruktur. Während der nächsten fünf Jahre arbeiten jeweils drei Teams parallel an einem Archiv, unterstützt durch Fachspezialist/innen aus Konservierung, Datenbankmanagement, Digitalisierung und Logistik."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Neben der physischen Konservierung von Vintage-Fotografien, Kontaktbögen, Diapositiven und Negativen, die je nach Material anders behandelt und gelagert werden müssen, ist die Sicherung von zahlreichen, teils stark gefährdeten Negativbeständen dringlich: Insbesondere vor 1970 belichtetes Filmmaterial besteht häufig aus Zellulose-Nitrat oder Azetat, dessen Zerfall sich durch klimatisierte Lagerung zwar verlangsamen, nicht aber aufhalten lässt. Die Fotostiftung digitalisiert ihre Bestände mittels Repro-Fotografie; Masterdateien werden im digitalen Langzeitarchiv gesichert, Abbildungen über das «Bildarchiv Online» öffentlich zugänglich gemacht. article_text:
Die Fotostiftung Schweiz startet ihr bislang grösstes Erschliessungsprojekt: Bis 2031 wird sie rund 160 Archive konservatorisch sichern, digitalisieren und der Öffentlichkeit zugänglich machen. Das auf fünf Jahre angelegte Grossprojekt bildet den Kern der strategischen Neuausrichtung der Stiftung.

Im Zentrum des Projekts steht die physische und inhaltliche Aufarbeitung der rund 160 Archive, welche die Fotostiftung im Auftrag des Bundes betreut und die zusammen geschätzt 3,5 Millionen Objekte umfassen. Für jedes Archiv wird die innere Ordnung festgestellt und sichtbar gemacht, die Fotografien werden erfasst und inhaltlich beschrieben, in archivtaugliche Materialien umgepackt und eine Auswahl durch Sicherungsdigitalisierungen für die Zukunft bewahrt. Parallel dazu erfolgen die Modernisierung der Depots und der Ausbau der digitalen Infrastruktur. Während der nächsten fünf Jahre arbeiten jeweils drei Teams parallel an einem Archiv, unterstützt durch Fachspezialist/innen aus Konservierung, Datenbankmanagement, Digitalisierung und Logistik.

Neben der physischen Konservierung von Vintage-Fotografien, Kontaktbögen, Diapositiven und Negativen, die je nach Material anders behandelt und gelagert werden müssen, ist die Sicherung von zahlreichen, teils stark gefährdeten Negativbeständen dringlich: Insbesondere vor 1970 belichtetes Filmmaterial besteht häufig aus Zellulose-Nitrat oder Azetat, dessen Zerfall sich durch klimatisierte Lagerung zwar verlangsamen, nicht aber aufhalten lässt. Die Fotostiftung digitalisiert ihre Bestände mittels Repro-Fotografie; Masterdateien werden im digitalen Langzeitarchiv gesichert, Abbildungen über das «Bildarchiv Online» öffentlich zugänglich gemacht. Die wachsende Anzahl digitaler Bildbestände aus hybriden Archiven bringt neue Herausforderungen mit sich. Das Projektteam nimmt sich ihrer an. Langfristig sollen verlässliche Bestandsdaten maschinenlesbar, normiert und über Permalinks dauerhaft zugänglich gemacht werden, sodass eine Vernetzung mit anderen wissenschaftlichen Daten gewährleistet werden kann.

Viele Negative, Dias, Prints und Objekte …

warten darauf neu digitalisiert und erfasst zu werden. (Fotos: © Fotostiftung)

Zu jedem bearbeiteten Archiv entsteht ein digitales Schaufenster von 100 Fotografien, das online zugänglich sein wird. Die Archive werden verschlagwortet. Neue Kontexte entstehen. Redaktionen, Ausstellungsmacher, Verlage, Nachwuchs-Fotografinnen, Historikerinnen, Wissenschaftler oder Kunstsammlerinnen nutzen die Datenbank. Sie bestellen Originale oder hochwertig angefertigte Ausstellungskopien und vertiefen sich in Dokumente, die viel über die Entstehung der Fotografien verraten – etwa über Auftraggeberinnen, über die Beziehung zwischen Autor und Motiv oder den Reiz, spontan den Auslöser zu drücken. Im Rahmen des Projekts werden solche Zeugnisse, Hintergründe und weiterführende Quellen in der Datenbank vermerkt.

Vor Ort im Foyer an der Grüzenstrasse 45 werden Besuchende fortlaufend über den Projektstand informiert. Bistro und Bibliothek bleiben geöffnet. Ab Juni 2027 zeigt eine erste Werkstattausstellung wichtige Sammlungsbereiche der Stiftung. Die digitale Vermittlung wird gestärkt. Aufgezeichnete Oral-History-Interviews ergänzen die monatliche Werkstatt-Veranstaltung «Out of the Box» und die dreimal jährlich stattfindende «Archives For Future», eine Reihe von Vorträgen und Gesprächen zu abgeschlossenen Archiven. Da der grosse Ausstellungsraum in Winterthur während der kommenden Jahre für die Archivarbeit benötigt wird, richtet die Fotostiftung ihre Ausstellungstätigkeit ab 2027 vermehrt extra muros aus. Kooperationen mit dem Kunstmuseum Basel, dem Historischen Museum Olten, dem Photoforum Pasquart und dem Kunstmuseum Thurgau sind unter Dach und Fach. So erreichen die Bestände der Fotostiftung schweizweit 2027 und in den Folgejahren ein wachsendes Publikum.

Das Projekt wird unterstützt vom Bundesamt für Kultur, den Kantonen Zürich, Thurgau und Tessin, der Stadt Winterthur sowie von privaten Förderern. Dazu gehören die Ernst Göhner Stiftung, die Giuseppe-Kaiser-Stiftung und die Anne-Marie-Schindler-Stiftung.

Neue Führung für die Neuausrichtung

Ein Führungsteam aus vier langjährigen Mitarbeiterinnen hat die operative Leitung der Fotostiftung Schweiz übernommen: Kerstin Camenisch (Administration), Madleina Deplazes (Archive & Sammlungen), Teresa Gruber (Ausstellungen & Vertiefung) und Katharina Rippstein (Digitalisierung & Bildnutzung). Mit «Bewahren in Bewegung» realisieren die Co-Direktorinnen mit ihrem Team nun das zentrale Vorhaben der Neuausrichtung: einen mehrjährigen Transformationsprozess für die nationale Gedächtnisinstitution der Schweizer Fotografie. (Foto: © Fotostiftung / Dominique Meienberg)

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures has rounded out the cast for its coming-of-age comedy Narcs , with three additions: Callan Farris ( Grimcutty ) has landed the third lead opposite Mason Thames and Ella Bright, with Lexi Minetree ( Elle ), and Josh Macqueen (upcoming Thunder Road ) also coming aboard.

Character details are being kept under wraps; the film’s plot also remains a mystery.

Slated for release in theaters on August 20, 2027, Narcs marks the directorial debut of John Phillips, whose writing credits include the R-rated comedies No Hard Feelings , Good Boys and Dirty Grandpa . Phillips is working from a script by Jordan & Justin Shipley, creators of the TBS comedy Wrecked , with a rewrite by Phillips & frequent collaborator Gene Stupnitsky, who’s producing through his Big Name Entertainment banner. Robert Lamonaca is exec producing via Big Name, alongside Phillips and Joseph Micucci.

Related Stories

Sony Pictures Lands Film Rights To Brett Bean's Bestselling Comic Book Series 'D'Orc'

Tom Holland And Drew Pearce Team On Sony Thriller 'Penthouse' With Billy17 And Point Of No Return Producing

Farris comes to Narcs with credits including the films Kings and Grimcutty , as well as Disney Channel’s Gabby Duran & The Unsittables and Disney Jr.’s cartoon The Rocketeer . He is repped by Coast to Coast Talent Group, Protégé Entertainment, and Myman Greenspan Fox.

Watch on Deadline

Best known for playing the title role in Prime Video’s Legally Blonde prequel series Elle , Minetree will next be seen in Neon’s horror film The Young People from Longlegs ‘ Osgood Perkins. She is repped by CAA, Framework Entertainment, and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

An Australian actor with credits like Motorheads and Black Snow , Macqueen’s next to be seen in The Sticks , a hockey drama series from Netflix and 21 Laps, and the AMC NASCAR drama Thunder Road . He is repped by Innovative Artists, Anonymous Content, and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman.

article_text:
Metropolis: more than four decades of street photography – in pictures

Metropolis: Street Photography 1985–2025 transitions from the tough, film-noir streets of 1980s New York, to the time surrounding the fall of the Berlin Wall, to the modern, colour-saturated, hard-shadowed geometry of contemporary Australian streets. Spanning classic monochrome grit and vivid colour abstraction, this remarkable collection examines how photographers have documented the relentless energy of our ever-changing cities. Ultimately, it is a celebration of the unscripted characters, strange encounters and the absurd comedy that unfolds when people share public space. On now until 17 November at The Photographic Gallery, Sydney

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我不相信给故事画上句号。我就是不这么做。”在日内瓦湖畔、Images Vevey图书奖颁奖典礼的下午，在一连串关于游泳的问题间隙，斯黛西·克拉尼茨（Stacy Kranitz）抛出了这句话。她在阿巴拉契亚山脉工作了17年——这条山脉绵延3,000多公里，从加拿大一直延伸到亚拉巴马州。或者说是20年，她有些犹豫。这本书的书名取自克劳德·伊利兄弟（Brother Claude Ely）的一首福音歌曲，这位五旬节派传教士正来自那些山脉。由莱内克·迪克斯特拉（Rineke Dijkstra）担任主席的评审团将大奖授予了这部作品；Éditions Images Vevey与美国出版商Terrible Baby于6月将其出版。贯穿始终的核心理念是：每一张图像都在一定程度上制造了它所宣称要描述的名声。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/family-standing-in-front-of-cabin-near-mt.-sterling-north-carolina-great-smoky-mountains-national-park-archive-1024x791.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Family standing in front of cabin, near Mt. Sterling, North Carolina © Great Smoky Mountains National Park Archive", "credit": "Blind Magazine", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在耶尼施博物馆（Musée Jenisch），这场展览将这一原则严格落到了实处。斯黛西·克拉尼茨在西弗吉尼亚州的一个山谷中拍摄的彩色照片，与1850年以来外来者对该地区拍摄的影像形成了对照。筹集资金的传教士、煤炭公司雇用的摄影师、农场安全管理局（Farm Security Administration）的特使、报道反贫困战争（War on Poverty）的记者：每一波来访者都带着使命而来，其取景框也早已预设好。由摄影师执导的一部纪录片占据了展陈的核心位置。“在美国，根本没有视觉素养，”她说，“没有人知道、理解或反思图像如何在世界上流通，有哪些不同的机制在起作用。没有人会去思考这些事情。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一切始于2013年一个周五的夜晚，在西弗吉尼亚州西哥伦比亚（West Columbia）。斯黛西·克拉尼茨应邀去一个男人的家中喝啤酒，不到一个小时的时间里，这个人就卷入了三场拳击斗殴，不仅砸了椅子，还一拳打在朋友多泽（Dozer）的脸上。他脖子后方纹着一个词：“红脖子”（Honkey）。律师哈里·考迪尔（Harry Caudill）大概会把帕特·格林（Pat Greene）归入他所谓的山谷“笨蛋”之列。而这位摄影师则一去再去，先是一个十年，接着又是一个十年。“对我来说，他真正认同自己是一个高地人，”她这样评价自己的东道主，“他真正体现了山地生活的生活理念。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "夏末的一天，在一条被改造成全地形车（ATV）小道的废弃露天煤矿上，在多泽喝了十几罐啤酒之后，斯黛西·克拉尼茨背着相机爬上了他的全地形车后座。书中的一张照片说明道出了其余的一切：“斯黛西和多泽在四轮车上，翻车前的一刻。”重达95公斤的多泽压在她身上；重达340公斤的四轮车则压在多泽身上。一个手肘擦伤。回到帕特家后，有人递给她一颗压碎的洛托布（Lortab）让她吸入以缓解疼痛。作为参与者而非仅仅旁观者，她从这个圈子的内部进行拍摄，带着这种拍摄方式所意味着的风险，以及它为她赢得的地位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "接着便是漫长历史，一本通过文献徐徐展开的书。为了逃离阶级制度，许多家庭离开欧洲，却发现自己成了契约劳工，于是爬上群山，在资本主义之外生活了一个世纪。随后，煤炭也循着山路追了上来。“他们简直是盗取了土地，”斯黛西·克拉尼茨说道，“他们根本不知道自己需要地契。没有人告诉他们需要地契。那么，是谁来决定他们需要地契的呢？是煤炭公司。”1964年4月24日，林登·约翰逊（Lyndon Johnson）坐在肯塔基州伊内兹（Inez）失业矿工汤姆·弗莱彻（Tom Fletcher）家的门廊上，这位矿工去年的收入约为400美元。这张照片成了反贫困战争的象征。弗莱彻于2004年在贫困中离世，被每隔十年就回来询问他是否依然贫穷的记者们折磨得精疲力竭。在全书的末尾，“剥夺词库”排列出了那些用来将这些人排除在人类契约之外的词汇，从“垃圾人”（waste article_text:
“I don’t believe in ending stories. I just don’t do it.” Stacy Kranitz drops the line by Lake Geneva, on the afternoon of the Images Vevey Book Award ceremony, between two questions about swimming. Seventeen years she has been working in Appalachia, the mountain range that runs more than 3,000 kilometers from Canada down to Alabama. Or twenty, she hesitates. The book takes its title from a gospel song by Brother Claude Ely, a Pentecostal preacher from those mountains. The jury chaired by Rineke Dijkstra crowned it; Éditions Images Vevey and the American publisher Terrible Baby brought it out in June. One idea governs the whole: every image manufactures a little of the reputation it claims to describe.

At the Musée Jenisch, the installation applies that principle to the letter. Stacy Kranitz’s color photographs, made in a West Virginia hollow, face the images produced about the region by outsiders since 1850. Missionaries raising funds, photographers on the payroll of the coal companies, envoys of the Farm Security Administration, reporters covering the War on Poverty: each wave arrived with its commission in hand and its framing already written. And a documentary film directed by the photographer holds the center of the display. “There’s no visual literacy in America,” she says. “Nobody knows, understands, or processes how images circulate in the world, the different kinds of apparatuses that are at play. Nobody thinks about this stuff.”

It all starts on a Friday night in 2013, in West Columbia, West Virginia. Stacy Kranitz is invited for a beer at the home of a man who, within the hour, gets into three fistfights, throws chairs and punches his friend Dozer in the face. On the back of his neck, a tattoo: “Honkey.” The lawyer Harry Caudill would have filed Pat Greene among what he called the “dullards” of the back hollows. The photographer, for her part, keeps coming back for a decade, then another. “To me, he really identifies as a mountaineer,” she says of her host. “He really embodies the idea of living mountain life.”

One late summer, on a strip mine reclaimed as an ATV trail, Stacy Kranitz climbs on behind Dozer, camera on her back, after a dozen beers for him. The caption of one picture in the book says the rest: “Stacy and Dozer on his four-wheeler, the moment before it flipped.” Dozer, 95 kilos, lands on her; the quad, 340 kilos, lands on Dozer. One bruised elbow. Back at Pat’s, someone hands her a crushed Lortab to snort for the pain. Participant as much as observer, she photographs from inside the circle, with the risks that implies and the standing it earns.

Then comes the long history, the one the book unfolds through documents. Families left Europe to escape a class system, found themselves indentured, climbed into the mountains and lived a century outside capitalism. Then coal climbed up after them. “They literally stole the land,” Stacy Kranitz says. “They didn’t know they needed to have deeds. Nobody told them they need to have deeds. So who decides that they need to have deeds? The coal companies.” On April 24, 1964, Lyndon Johnson sat on the porch of Tom Fletcher, an unemployed miner in Inez, Kentucky, who had earned about 400 dollars the previous year. The picture became the emblem of the War on Poverty. Fletcher died poor in 2004, worn out by the reporters who came back every ten years to ask whether he still was. At the end of the volume, a “lexicon of dispossession” lines up the words coined to keep these people outside the human contract, from waste people to trailer trash . Four centuries of vocabulary, a single function.

Then there is Harry Caudill, the dark heart of the affair and the subject of the film. His essay “The Rape of the Appalachians,” published in The Atlantic in 1962, and Night Comes to the Cumberlands a year later, turned America’s attention to a region bled dry by coal. Twenty years on, the same man explained poverty by genetics, invited the eugenicist William Shockley to his Kentucky home and floated cash bounties for sterilization. Stacy Kranitz unearthed the footage in which he makes that claim on camera. On November 29, 1990, facing Pine Mountain, Caudill shot himself; his farewell letter is reproduced in the book. One detail from the same archive amuses his Swiss publishers. “He mentions the Swiss. He says, we want to do it like the Swiss,” the photographer reports. The film, for its part, turns back on its own author and asks the question that holds for the entire project: what does an image of poverty do, once it is loose in the world?

Next comes J. D. Vance, whose Hillbilly Elegy (2016) recounts an Appalachian childhood and hands his own people the blame for their decline. Stacy Kranitz places the two men in the same frame and notes the coincidence: Pat’s daughter was taken by child protective services just as Vance was named running mate. “It’s my form of politics,” she says of that montage. “I don’t know why we’re not talking about eugenics more. We are still lurking in that conversation in every direction.” A Nieman Fellow, she is spending the year at Harvard, where she studies eugenics and pronatalism.

The book saves its most troubling object for last. In 2016, a photograph of Pat shirtless in his yard became a meme: “Poor southern conservatives have been voting Republican for generations. And they’re still poor.” Pat, with a criminal record, cannot vote. The essayist Whitney Phillips devotes one of the book’s texts to it. Stacy Kranitz has known the mechanism since 2012, when CNN ran her images of a Pentecostal snake handler and a Ku Klux Klan gathering under the headline “Everyday life in Appalachia.” It took a week on the phone to get the headline changed. “Photography has done a lot of harm to that region,” she says. “That doesn’t mean that you can’t or shouldn’t.” She describes the model that governs the news: “A flood, an earthquake, some disaster, we descend on the region, everyone’s there at the same time, and then we abandon ship.” Her work does the opposite, slowly. “Art allowed me to slow down and tell the story over a much longer period of time. You can’t really do it in journalism.”

So she stays. Stacy Kranitz went through every caption with Pat Greene, recorder on the table. “I really needed him to see what I wrote,” she says, “to make sure that he agreed with the context, with the way that it was being used in the book.” The last pictures date from March 2026. As the book went to press, Pat was in jail, with no one to post bail. “We love to put poor people in jail for no good reason,” she says. Five weeks of silence, then a rehab center, where she was able to visit him. “I’ve never seen him more contemplative,” says the photographer, who has always known him in survival mode. The book ends in the dark; life has turned since. Such is the advantage of stories that keep going. “I will probably be there for a long time, and I will not be leaving.”

Ain’t No Grave Gonna Hold My Body Down by Stacy Kranitz is published by Terrible Baby / Éditions Images Vevey and available for $70. The exhibition at the Musée Jenisch, part of the Images Vevey Biennial , runs through September 27, 2026.

article_text:
Art Basel Paris si farà regolarmente: mentre in Francia continuano le proteste legate al costo della vita, alle condizioni della scuola e al deterioramento dei servizi pubblici – e dopo un fine settimana segnato anche da scontri, saccheggi e incendi – gli organizzatori della fiera hanno confermato che l’edizione 2026 al Grand Palais di Parigi procederà secondo programma, rafforzando però le misure di sicurezza.

La quinta edizione parigina della manifestazione riunirà 211 espositori provenienti da 41 Paesi. L’Avant-Première è prevista il 20 ottobre, le giornate VIP il 21 e 22, mentre l’apertura al pubblico sarà dal 23 al 25 ottobre. «La fiera si svolgerà come previsto e sono in corso gli ultimi preparativi», ha confermato un portavoce ad Artnet.

Domenica, 18 ottobre, dopo le manifestazioni del giorno precedente, Art Basel ha scritto ai propri VIP per comunicare l’adozione di «Comprehensive safety measures» – misure di sicurezza complete. Tra gli interventi indicati figurano barriere anti-intrusione installate intorno al Grand Palais per impedire l’accesso di veicoli non autorizzati nelle aree pedonali circostanti e un aumento del personale incaricato di sorvegliare il perimetro della fiera 24 ore su 24. Già le normali disposizioni di accesso prevedono controlli tramite metal detector e ispezione visiva delle borse per tutti i visitatori.

Una Francia attraversata dalle proteste

La rassicurazione arriva dopo settimane di mobilitazioni che hanno avuto tra i protagonisti soprattutto studenti e giovani e che, partite anche dalle condizioni degli edifici scolastici e dalla carenza di personale e risorse nell’istruzione, si sono progressivamente intrecciate con rivendicazioni più ampie sul costo della vita, sui salari e sui servizi pubblici.

Il 17 ottobre, tra 550mila e 800mila persone, secondo le diverse stime riportate dalle agenzie internazionali, hanno partecipato a manifestazioni in circa 110 cortei in tutta la Francia. La maggior parte delle proteste si è svolta pacificamente ma in diverse città gruppi più radicali hanno dato vita a scontri con la polizia e incendi. Nei giorni successivi il numero degli arresti comunicati dalle autorità ha superato quota 2mila.

Uno degli episodi più gravi ha riguardato Limoges, dove il municipio ottocentesco, monumento storico inaugurato nel 1883, è stato incendiato al termine delle manifestazioni. Il tetto e buona parte della facciata sono crollati, insieme alla torre dell’orologio. Il prefetto dell’Alta Vienne, Maurice Barate , ha parlato di una «Catastrofe per il patrimonio», distinguendo esplicitamente gli autori dell’incendio dai manifestanti che avevano partecipato al corteo.

Il clima di tensione ha già prodotto qualche conseguenza sulla programmazione culturale parigina. Il Jeu de Paume, per esempio, ha cancellato un’apertura domenicale della mostra di Stan Douglas per il rischio di nuove proteste. Per il momento, però, gli effetti più ampi sul sistema dell’arte appaiono circoscritti.

Intanto però nella mattinata di oggi i manifestanti hanno blocato l’accesso al Louvre, come annunciato dalla direzione del Museo e dai sindacati all’agenzia France Presse. Il blocco è stato promosso da una cinquantina di studenti dell’École du Louvre, scuola superiore di storia dell’arte ospitata nel palazzo dove si trova anche l’omonimo museo, per solidarizzare con i liceali: «Siamo fieri di annunciarvi il blocco del più grande museo del mondo», si legge in un volantino affisso nei pressi del museo.

Il disagio sociale oltre i confini francesi

Le mobilitazioni francesi si inseriscono in un contesto europeo più ampio. Negli stessi giorni proteste e, in alcuni casi, scontri si sono verificati anche in Italia, Belgio, Portogallo e Albania, con rivendicazioni differenti ma spesso accomunate dalla pressione esercitata dal costo della vita, dalle condizioni dei servizi pubblici e dalle difficoltà – economiche e non solo – percepite dalle generazioni più giovani.

In Italia, a Bologna, Torino, Brescia e Bergamo si sono registrati episodi di violenza. A Milano, in particolare, gruppi di persone incappucciate hanno danneggiato e saccheggiato esercizi commerciali nel centro cittadino, con la polizia che è intervenuta con lacrimogeni e idranti.

Ridurre questo quadro esclusivamente agli episodi di vandalismo rischia tuttavia di oscurare l’origine più ampia delle mobilitazioni e appiattirne le dinamiche. Se le violenze costituiscono una componente minoritaria rispetto alle centinaia di migliaia di persone che hanno manifestato in maniera pacifica, rendono comunque più evidente un disagio che, in vari modi e diverse espressioni, attraversa tutta la società europea, assumendo forme non sempre sovrapponibili e che andrebbero considerate nella loro complessità.

Anche la condanna degli episodi di violenza deve essere accompagnata da una domanda più scomoda: fino a che punto è possibile analizzare la distruttività che emerge nelle strade separandola dall’economia generale della violenza nella quale queste stesse società sono immerse? Viviamo in un sistema che rende quotidianamente visibile e politicamente praticabile una capacità distruttiva enorme – dai genocidi perpetrati da apparati militari, alle forme meno evidenti di esclusione economica e sociale – mentre tende a considerare la violenza che affiora nelle condotte delle proprie periferie sociali come un fenomeno completamente altro, improvviso e incomprensibile. Aprire questa prospettiva non significa stabilire equivalenze né interpretare la protesta violenta come una conseguenza inevitabile. Rimane infatti fondamentale interrogare il contesto nel quale la rivolta prende forma: una condanna che riduca al silenzio questa domanda rischia di descrivere soltanto l’atto finale, lasciando fuori il sistema di tensioni che accende la stessa rivolta.

Art Basel tra mercato globale e instabilità geopolitica

In Francia il presidente Emmanuel Macron ha riconosciuto la legittimità delle preoccupazioni legate all’aumento del costo della vita e al deterioramento dei servizi, al contempo condannando le violenze e annunciando un confronto con studenti, insegnanti, sindacati e altri rappresentanti sociali. Ma per Art Basel, la situazione parigina pone una questione che va oltre l’organizzazione di questa singola edizione. L’ampliamento del marchio in una piattaforma globale – oggi presente tra Basilea, Miami Beach, Parigi, Hong Kong e Doha – comporta inevitabilmente un rapporto sempre più stretto con condizioni politiche e geopolitiche molto differenti.

Il tema della sicurezza e della sua percezione ha accompagnato anche l’esordio di Art Basel Qatar nel febbraio 2026. La fiera ha debuttato a Doha in una regione segnata da forti tensioni, presentando 87 gallerie provenienti da 31 Paesi e territori ( qui il nostro report ).

Almeno nei numeri diffusi dagli organizzatori, quella situazione non sembra aver compromesso in maniera rilevante la partecipazione. La prima edizione ha registrato oltre 17mila visitatori, con rappresentanti di più di 85 musei e fondazioni internazionali e una presenza di collezionisti provenienti non solo dall’area MENASA ma anche da Europa, Asia, Africa e Americhe. Le gallerie hanno inoltre riportato vendite in diverse fasce di prezzo.

I numeri dell’affluenza però possono non essere indicativi dello stato delle questioni legate al contesto in cui una fiera opera, né permettono di misurare da soli la percezione della sicurezza da parte dei partecipanti. Mostrano però la capacità di Art Basel di mantenere una mobilità internazionale significativa anche all’interno di scenari ad alto tasso di imprevedibilità.

Il Grand Palais mentre fuori la città protesta

A Parigi questa contraddizione sarà particolarmente visibile. Da una parte il Grand Palais, con oltre 200 gallerie, con collezionisti internazionali e con opere che interessano le fasce più alte del mercato. Dall’altra una città nella quale una parte della popolazione manifesta contro le disuguaglianze sociali.

Una distanza che alcuni operatori del sistema dell’arte presenti in città hanno già rilevato. La curatrice italiana Valentina Buzzi ha raccontato di essere uscita da un’installazione nel Marais mentre nell’aria erano ancora presenti i lacrimogeni, per entrare poco dopo in una galleria, definendo «Surreale» il passaggio tra le due dimensioni. James Michael Shaeffer , direttore della Galerie Chantal Crousel, ha invece invitato i visitatori arrivati per Art Basel a guardare anche alle rivendicazioni degli studenti e non soltanto alle immagini di incendi e danneggiamenti.

A rendere ancora più evidente questa distanza contribuirà la densità di appuntamenti culturali concentrati a Parigi negli stessi giorni. Dal 19 al 25 ottobre la città ospiterà infatti, oltre ad Art Basel Paris, un fitto calendario di fiere e manifestazioni : da Paris Internationale a Design Miami Paris, da AKAA – Also Known As Africa ad ASIA NOW, passando per OFFSCREEN, Moderne Art Fair e la prima edizione europea di Post-Fair. Design, fotografia, arte contemporanea, scene africane e asiatiche, gallerie emergenti e grandi operatori internazionali andranno a scandire un percorso che attraverserà quartieri, palazzi storici e spazi indipendenti. Muoversi in città durante questa settimana potrebbe risultare dunque ancora più straniante. Nelle stesse strade si incroceranno collezionisti, curatori, galleristi e visitatori arrivati da tutto il mondo per uno dei momenti più importanti dell’anno per il mercato dell’arte, mentre poco distante i manifesti dei cortei continueranno a sfilare.

Art Basel Paris aprirà quindi regolarmente. Ma le barriere attorno al Grand Palais e l’aumento della sorveglianza raccontano qualcosa che va oltre questa settimana fieristica: per un operatore multinazionale dell’arte, la sicurezza è diventata una delle variabili attraverso cui il mercato globale deve misurarsi, in una società attraversata da crisi economiche, politiche e culturali sempre più difficili da lasciare fuori dalle porte.

(Photo by Cindy Ord/Getty Images for FLC)", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Six weeks later, the film is now opening in about 800 theaters across North America and projecting a debut of up to $8 million – practically a blockbuster figure for a documentary.
