article_text:
Oscar season boils down to crafting a winning narrative. Studios and publicists are tactical in selecting the right festival, the right venue, and the right occasion to unveil their wares and carefully provide audiences the appropriate context for a film to be appreciated and, if executed successfully, awarded. But A24 is broadcasting a somewhat divergent approach with its Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ”: see it, especially before you find out anything else about it.

After being produced in secret over three years, the film was first revealed to the world with a highly speculated-about mystery screening at Telluride Film Festival. There, the film’s directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , implored the sold-out audience to not spoil its most discombobulating twists. “You Can See Everything” electrified what had been a somewhat quiet festival season, with awards prognosticators instantly canonizing the showstopper as a serious threat to become the first documentary to land a best picture Oscar nomination.

Six weeks later, the film is now opening in about 800 theaters across North America and projecting a debut of up to $8 million – practically a blockbuster figure for a documentary. Two more sold-out screenings have also come, at New York Film Festival and the Academy Museum in Los Angeles. The screening at NYFF (where A24 also kicked off the virality-mindset marketing of “Marty Supreme” last year) was such a hot ticket that a Film at Lincoln Center programmer shared a post lamenting that she couldn’t manage to get a seat. And though NYFF typically shares videos of its Q&As online, the organization made an agreement with A24 to withhold posting the post-screening conversation between Fielder, Oppenheim and festival director Dennis Lim until after opening weekend.

That atypical gesture of confidentiality matches the co-directors’ hope that audiences won’t spoil how the documentary unfolds, inviting its few viewers so far into an air of secrecy that began with its confidential production circumstances, already mythologized among the press and Fielder acolytes. As Fielder has been shared in Q&As, “You Can See Everything” first began with a seven-person crew visiting the home of Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, in 2023. The small group documented Holmes in the month leading up to her 11-year prison sentence for wire fraud and defrauding investors in her tech start-up Theranos.

The cat very nearly stayed in the bag over three years, apart from a 2025 report by independent journalist Jeff Sneider detailing a rumor about Fielder working on a project that involved meeting Holmes while she was in prison. When IndieWire sent a text to a source close to the project about the piece, they did not initially respond. Later, speaking in-person, they claimed that they didn’t write back because they were legally barred from doing so. A24 declined to comment for this story.

Nondisclosure agreements aren’t an unusual part of above-the-line workers and crew members agreeing to come aboard a film production, though the scope of their contents can vastly vary. Per The Wall Street Journal and Variety , NDAs were employed on Fielder’s HBO docuseries “The Rehearsal,” which sees the comedian giving everyday people the opportunity to rehearse difficult conversations with hired actors and elaborate sets. While some subjects have gone on to break those contracts, the series was largely able to preserve its biggest week-to-week reveals. But, perhaps more essentially, they also limit viewers’ avenues to gain clarity on Fielder’s signature ability to push the limits of ordinary behavior in highly constructed circumstances, leaving viewers to figure where one begins and the other ends on their own.

With “You Can See Everything,” Fielder also finds a kindred spirit with Oppenheim, whose documentary work like HBO’s series “Ren Faire” and the FX feature “Spermworld” hinged on the formal premise of directly inviting subjects into the filmmaking process. Across his work, Oppenheim collaborates with the people being documented, helping them craft reenactments of particularly consequential moments in their lives and, sometimes, even venturing into expressionistic compositions that break from vérité and stylishly reflect the subjects’ psyches. Both Fielder and Oppenheim’s open reconstruction of documentary reality drives “You Can See Everything” through its epic, near-three-hour running time, particularly through the film’s latter half, after Holmes goes to prison and the crew is forced to rethink how to continue the project with limited access to her.

It is in that turn where “You Can See Everything” becomes a truly bizarre awards player, with the production inviting a well-known actor aboard. In pre-screening introductions, Fielder and Oppenheim have implored audiences to not discuss this actor’s identity or the nature of their involvement, but this hasn’t stopped some awards prognosticators from predicting the film in supporting performance categories. IndieWire understands that the publicists behind the awards campaign for “You Can See Everything” are not providing specific guidance to awards predictors on whether to conceal this performer’s identity.

Some movies have pulled off keeping an actor’s involvement largely unknown until a film’s release; think Kevin Spacey’s serial killer in “Se7en,” or Matt Damon’s castaway coward in “Interstellar.” But the modern age of Oscar jockeying hasn’t seen such a film then parlay that secrecy into a nomination. And this isn’t even to mention the especially odd idea of an acting nomination coming from a documentary, no matter how many recreations there are in it.

The especially strange awards prospects for “You Can See Everything,” with unique qualifiers across several awards bodies , seem a bizarre aftershock to the film itself, which teases viewers to put a finger on what’s real and what’s not. Even Fielder, who often hovers above his work with a removed, Machiavellian pose, has claimed that question even stumps him. As he put it during his Telluride Q&A , “I still am not sure to this day what I experienced.” Taken in a media landscape defined by aggressive promotional gauntlets and hand-fed readings of each film, the film’s ability to totally bemuse viewers is an irreplaceable commodity — even if it’s a first impression that has been as aggressively engineered as any other awards player’s.

A24’s “You Can See Everything” is now playing in theaters.
excerpt_original: The Elizabeth Holmes documentary has managed to keep a lid on its biggest twists since being revealed to the world in September. Now comes the spotlight of a wide release and awards season.

article_text:
It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV.

The FCC’s “financial interest and syndication” rules forced TV networks to buy shows from superproducers like Norman Lear and Grant Tinker rather than making them in-house. And ever since the FCC did away with fin-syn 30 years ago, producers and agents have been longing for its return.

Related Stories

‘Musk’ Director Alex Gibney Confirms Universal Wavered in Planning Overseas Release, Says He Tried to Interview Elon Musk: ‘His Response Was Writing “Gibney Is a Douche”’

Now, with momentum building behind a U.S. film incentive, they are hoping the moment is ripe to recreate fin-syn for the streaming era. They argue it would bring a jolt of creativity and a spirit of enterprise to a business stuck in a creative slump.

The major agencies — WME , CAA and UTA — announced last week that they are forming a coalition with production companies including Imagine Entertainment and Legendary to push for legislation that would force streamers to buy at least 50% of their original content from independent producers. The legislation would also limit the length of licensing terms, reviving secondary markets that have largely withered away.

Their message is that Hollywood ails not only from runaway production, but also from a consolidated ecosystem that limits creativity and makes it harder for producers, writers and actors to profit from their labor.

“The tax incentive may change where the production shoots, but it doesn’t change who owns and profits from it,” argued Ken Ziffren, co-founder of Ziffren Brittenham LLP, who has been campaigning for a restoration of fin-syn for decades. “We think the tax legislation only goes so far to help our industry and it’s not a complete effort, and it can’t be a complete effort, unless it’s paired with a modernized ownership framework.”

Jeff Sagansky, a producer, investor and longtime fin-syn supporter , argued that overseas incentives are not the only reason that U.S. production jobs are going away.

“They’re also going away because of the way the streaming business has consolidated around four players,” he said. “They act as an oligopoly. They’ve got incredible pricing power,” saying the streamers are ordering 30-40% fewer hours of programming than they were a few years ago.

Getting the idea through Congress will be an uphill battle, and will face adamant opposition from Netflix, Amazon and the other streaming platforms. The effort also has the potential to sow division within an industry that has united behind the goal of passing the first-ever federal film incentive.

Supporters wanted to some version of their ideas into the tax credit bill that was introduced to much fanfare in September. But while they had some positive meetings, they were ultimately rebuffed. They are now aiming for 2027, when Democrats are expected to take control of at least one of the houses of Congress.

Rep. Laura Friedman, a co-author of the tax incentive as well as a former producer, said in a statement that she sympathizes with producers’ concerns about industry consolidation and the threat to diverse voices in entertainment.

“My focus right now is on passing our bipartisan national film tax credit bill to put film and television workers back on the job, but I look forward to continuing to work with stakeholders to ensure the industry is vibrant for the future,” she said.

The Streaming Innovation Alliance, which includes Netflix and other streamers, issued a statement on Thursday calling the proposal a package of “blunt government mandates” that would “only dampen production and discourage creative risk-taking.”

The Federal Communications Commission adopted the fin-syn rules in 1970, when there were only three TV networks. The rules prevented networks from owning syndication rights in their shows, and later, from owning shows that aired in primetime. The rules are credited with leading to an era of groundbreaking TV, including “All in the Family,” “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and “The Cosby Show.”

The repeal of the rules in the mid-90s spurred a wave of vertical integration, as Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC and Viacom acquired CBS.

Arguing that the end of fin-syn had killed off independent production, a group called the Coalition for Program Diversity urged the FCC to reinstate a version of it. In 2002, the coalition — led by Ziffren — sought a new regulation that 25% of primetime programming come from independent producers. In a deregulatory era, such pleas fell on deaf ears.

Nowadays, streamers typically either make shows themselves or buy from the handful of other major studios. When they do buy from indie producers, they typically take all rights for 10-20 years, locking the producers out of the option of selling into secondary markets.

Mark Vahradian, producer of the “Transformers” franchise and other films, argued that streamers are so powerful that they can dictate those terms, and that dynamic ultimately hurts consumers.

“There’s no incentive for the creators to go out and build something brand new,” said Vahradian, a founding member of Producers United. “That’s why they’re only making sequels and franchise titles. They own those and have no motivation to say ‘Why don’t we do something new?’”

For years there wasn’t much opportunity to do anything about it. But with President Trump vowing to “save” Hollywood from a dramatic downturn, fin-syn supporters see an opening.

The initiative would require an act of Congress, as the FCC’s ambit is limited to the public airwaves.

Andrew Long, a senior fellow at the Free State Foundation, a free-market think tank, argued that the streaming marketplace is far more diversified now than the three-network era of the 1970s.

“It’s hard to find factual predicate that would justify this kind of government intervention in the video distribution marketplace in 2026,” Long said, adding that it could raise First Amendment concerns. “I think there would be high scrutiny, and I think that given the state of the marketplace and the options available, it might not pass muster.”

But Rich Shuter, head of business affairs at UTA, argued that consolidation leaves his agency’s clients without much leverage — and viewers without much choice.

“We’re going back to a situation where you have these streaming conglomerates controlling all the content the country is viewing,” Shuter said. “They’re determining what is being produced.”

Shuter said that more risk-taking will lead to a more vibrant ecosystem.

“We don’t want to stall the federal tax credit from being passed as quickly as possible,” he said. “We hope the administration and Congress recognize this is a supplemental benefit.”

Après les Conversations photographiques lancées à Arles l’été passé, Sandisk™ et Fisheye s’associent de nouveau et proposent des balades visuelles. Pensées comme des ateliers de création collective, celles-ci auront lieu au cœur de La Villette, à l’occasion du Salon Photo & Vidéo.

Sandisk™ s’associe de nouveau à Fisheye et présente ses balades visuelles, dont voici les deux formulaires d’inscription . Au nombre de quatre et accueillant cinq à six participants, elles auront lieu les 10 et 11 octobre 2026, à 14h et 17h , lors du Salon Photo & Vidéo, à La Villette, auquel vous pourrez accéder gratuitement grâce au code FSEYE26. Celles du samedi s’articuleront autour de la vidéo et seront animées par Lucas Troadec , photographe et vidéaste qui interroge comment les espaces façonnent l’identité. Celles du dimanche feront la part belle à la photographie et seront portées par Diane Moyssan, photographe qui travaille notamment dans les univers du luxe, de la mode et du lifestyle . Toutes seront néanmoins traversées par un thème commun : le mouvement.

Concevoir une œuvre commune

Au début de ces ateliers d’une durée de 1h30, les participants rencontreront leur animateur qui les aidera à régler le boîtier qu’ils apporteront afin d’optimiser la prise de vue. Il leur donnera également des conseils artistiques pour mieux aborder la thématique. Après cela, ils sillonneront librement le parc de la Villette dans lequel ils utiliseront les modes les plus exigeants de leur appareil, à savoir la rafale haute vitesse en RAW et le slow motion haute fréquence d’images et 4K. S’ils nécessitent un matériel performant, ils requièrent tout autant de cartes fiables et adaptées, qui correspondent justement à celles développées par Sandisk™ et qui leur seront prêtées pour l’événement.

À l’issue de cette déambulation, toutes et tous se réuniront pour immortaliser une zone commune, au même moment, selon un angle différent. À la manière de Barbara Probst, les images seront ensuite assemblées, puis projetées sur un écran installé au stand Fisheye . Les co-créations pourront être relayées sur nos plateformes.

Pour vous inscrire, il suffit de cliquer sur ce lien pour le samedi ou celui-ci pour le dimanche , et d’indiquer le modèle de votre boîtier. En participant à l’un de ces ateliers, vous bénéficierez d’un code promo exclusif de 20 % de réduction sur l’ensemble des cartes du site Sandisk™, dans la limite de 500 € d’achat maximum. En outre, Sandisk™ et Fisheye organisent le jeu-concours gratuit Lucky Scan. Ce dernier consiste en un tirage au sort qui aura lieu à la fin du salon et permettra de remporter des produits Sandisk™. Au cours de cette édition du Salon Photo & Vidéo, vous pourrez également participer à une chasse au trésor de Boby.

article_text:
Welcome to The Film Stage Presents! Today we’re speaking with Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Daniel Kraus about his novel Whalefall and the new film of the same name (which he co-wrote with director Brian Duffield).

We chat about Whalefall , adapting it from book to screen, his recent Pulitzer win for his novel Angel Down , and other underrated sea survivor movies. Among them are All Is Lost , White Squall , and In the Heart of the Sea .

Additional topics discussed include the differences between books and movies, how the whale in Whalefall is actually a setting and not a villain, and the survival books we read as kids ( The Cay by Theodore Taylor, Hatchet by Gary Paulsen, Lord of the Flies by William Golding).

There are mentions of the great Walter Hill film Southern Comfort and the great Carroll Ballard film The Black Stallion . Alfonso Cuarón’s Gravity also comes up, which Kraus feels is the best comp to Whalefall .

"作为一个曾眼睁睁看着亲近之人被阿尔茨海默病夺走神智的人，《海上女王》让我感到格外揪心，尽管它在某些情节的处理上略显零散。情感是真挚的，哪怕故事有时确实显得迷失在茫茫大海中。阿曼达将丈夫（也是萨拉的父亲）留在纽卡斯尔后所处的地理配置令人困惑。与此同时，萨拉在纽卡斯尔与新朋友和潜在的新恋情一起非常迅速地重启了生活，编剧兼导演汉默在剪辑中将萨拉与同龄人萌芽中的恋情，与莱斯莉精神状况的恶化及与伴侣的疏离进行了平行对比。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "电影开场时，阿曼达正上门探望莱斯莉，却撞见马丁正试图与一个神情恍惚、眼神迷离、俯卧在床上的莱斯莉发生性关系。这已经不是第一次发生这种事了，阿曼达曾多次恳求马丁住手。但药柜里的伟哥却表明事实并非如此，他一而再再而三地这么做，而阿曼达则一直在要求他停下。", "translated": true}, "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "马丁坚称莱斯莉——这位曾经备受赞誉、才华横溢、如今却在精神、情感和身体上逐渐失语的画家——正在享受这些亲密接触。毕竟他们已经结婚19年了。当阿曼达报警并将官方卷入这一局势时，这段伴侣关系瞬间分崩离析。随之而来的便是关于他们是否应该继续分居以及是否将莱斯莉送进养老院的种种疑问。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "而这最终正是发生的事情，莱斯莉在那里与其他患者建立了一种不恰当的纽带，以填补马丁缺席后的空白。不过，编剧兼导演汉默淡化了这一情境中固有的情节剧色彩，同时以一种振奋人心的手持摄影亲密感来拍摄各个场景，无论是在马丁和莱斯莉的公寓里，还是在各大医院中。（与此同时，摄影师阿道夫·韦洛索为伦敦披上了一层美丽褪色的日光。）远非刻板冷静的构图，强加给莱斯莉的强奸检验包检查令人心碎且倍受侮辱，尤其是她根本不知道发生了什么，也完全不明白为什么要把窥阴器插进她体内。在哪个世界里马丁会强奸自己的妻子？", article_text:
Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Berlin Film Festival . Greenwich Entertainment releases “ Queen at Sea ” in theaters starting Friday, October 30.

Lance Hammer was the toast of the town in 2008 with his hard-hitting, Mississippi-set coming-of-age drama “ Ballast .” The Dardennes-esque vérité portrait of lives careening from loss and economic hardship won two awards at the Sundance Film Festival that year — including Best Director for Hammer — and received multiple Film Independent Spirit and Gotham award nominations.

And then, poof: Hammer was never heard from again.

He has now returned, almost two decades later, with an extremely upsetting but compassionate moral drama about agency amid dementia, titled “Queen at Sea.” It stars Juliette Binoche as a woman desperate and panicked to take care of her ailing mother, Leslie (Anna Calder-Marshall, absolutely shattering in her specificity toward the sickness’ toll), who is slipping deeper into the illness. Leslie’s grasp of time, memory, and function is vanishing in the multi-story London flat she shares with her husband of 19 years, Martin (a brutally heartbreaking Tom Courtenay). Meanwhile, Amanda (Binoche), an academic on sabbatical, is going through a separation herself — from her husband in Newcastle, and now she’s forced to bring her daughter, Sara (Florence Hunt), with her back to London to check in on her mother.

But when Amanda catches her stepfather, Martin, in a compromising position with Leslie, another separation sets into motion, with Leslie potentially about to be lost in an elder-care system that’s frightening and scary for the patient, and a kind of emotional death sentence for her and her loved ones.

As someone who’s watched a close loved one lose themselves to Alzheimer’s disease, I found “Queen at Sea” to be especially bruising, even despite some of its patchier plot notes. The emotions are there, even if the story is, well, lost at sea at times. The geographical configuration surrounding Amanda, having left behind a husband (and Sara’s father) in Newcastle, is confusing. Meanwhile, Sara has very quickly restarted her life in Newcastle with new friends and a potential new flame, as writer/director Hammer draws parallel comparisons in the edit between Sara’s blooming relationship with a classmate, and Leslie’s mental deterioration and estrangement from her own partner.

When the movie begins, Amanda is on a house call to check on Leslie, and walks in on Martin attempting to have sex with a dazed-out, addled-eyed Leslie prostrate on the bed. This is not the first time this has happened, and it’s an occurrence Amanda has implored Martin to knock off. But the Viagra in his medicine cabinet suggests otherwise, that he keeps going back for more, that Amanda keeps asking him to stop.

Dementia dramas like Sarah Polley’s wounding “Away from Her” (wherein Julie Christie’s husband Grant Anderson basically sets her up in a nursing home to counteract his own infidelities) and Michael Haneke’s Oscar-winning “Amour” (the harshest of this fleet of films) tend to center close-up on the relations between an Alzheimer’s patient and her partner, and how these relationships break down when there are fewer past and present memories to found them on.

Hammer’s film introduces profound new questions and issues about consent into the formula — is Leslie agreeing on some level to have sex with her husband? Is the only pleasure in her winnowing life to be denied? Can a person with dementia consent to having sex? Leslie’s instincts now are narrowed to the primal: food, water, sleep, and, naturally, sex. So where do all these leftover feelings go when the body containing them is now only a vessel for a going mind?

Martin insists that Leslie — a once-celebrated and very talented painter now slowly going mute, mentally and emotionally and physically — is enjoying these encounters. They’ve been married for 19 years, after all, and when Amanda calls the police and introduces authorities into the situation, the couple is suddenly torn asunder. Then arise questions about whether they should continue to be separated and whether to place Leslie in a home.

Which is eventually what happens, and where Leslie forms an inappropriate bond with another patient to fill the Martin void. Writer/director Hammer, though, downplays the melodrama inherent to this scenario, even while shooting sequences, whether in Martin and Leslie’s apartment or in various hospitals, with a bracing handheld intimacy. (Cinematographer Adolpho Veloso, meanwhile, bathes London in a beautifully faded daylight.) Far from sterilely composed, a rape kit examination forced upon Leslie is harrowing and demeaning, especially as she has no idea what’s going on and no clue why a speculum is being inserted into her. In what world could Martin have raped his wife?

Binoche, who has been giving committed and emotionally controlled performances for years lately, including in films by Haneke , gives one of her most unsentimental and gripping performances at this stage in her career in “Queen at Sea.” An emotional phone call to her soon-to-be ex-husband lays bare to blanched vulnerability as she dials the last person she would prefer not to call, but the one she is forced to anyway. Interior lives outside those determined by this situation may be lacking, but Leslie’s isn’t. Amanda’s mother seems to activate when given the chance to paint at a nursing home, an aseptic and terrible place for which everyone in the family seems to be awkwardly auditioning.

The great British actor Courtenay, most recently memorable in the similarly memory-impaired marriage portrait “45 Years” opposite Charlotte Rampling, is quite devastating as a husband scrambling for answers and to legitimize his own place in Leslie’s life. The one element that doesn’t quite land, and seems quite literally chopped into the film, is Florence Hunt as Amanda’s daughter. Hammer seems to be trying to signal that she may be headed for her own future mental ruin by intercutting her first romance with scenes of Martin and Leslie’s last. It’s a noble idea, but it ends up feeling like scraps from an earlier draft.

Ultimately, though, anyone who’s endured what Amanda, or Leslie, or Martin do in this movie will find something to relate to and feel toward. Hammer spares no hard truths and offers no pat feelings with regard to how these people are bound to end up and what dementia ultimately does to them. Let’s just say hope is at a shortage. But the actors help carry Hammer’s message — and make it unforgettable.

Grade: B+

“Queen at Sea” premiered at the 2026 Berlin Film Festival. Greenwich Entertainment opens the film starting Friday, October 30.

title_original: “It’s Cringy For Me to See Myself”: Sofia Coppola on Making Marie Antoinette
editorial_title_zh: “看到自己让我觉得挺肉麻的”：索菲亚·科波拉谈创作《绝代艳后》幕后纪录片
editorial_excerpt_zh: 2024年4月，索菲亚·科波拉（Sofia Coppola）失去了母亲埃莉诺（Eleanor）。这位科波拉家族中被索菲亚形容为“酷”、如定海神针般的女性，既是一位骄傲的母亲，也是一位骄傲的妻子。她的丈夫弗朗西斯（Francis）和女儿索菲亚曾拍出电影史上最具印象深刻（且风格迥异）的两份…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "2024年4月，索菲亚·科波拉（Sofia Coppola）失去了母亲埃莉诺（Eleanor）。这位科波拉家族中被索菲亚形容为“酷”、如定海神针般的女性，既是一位骄傲的母亲，也是一位骄傲的妻子。她的丈夫弗朗西斯（Francis）和女儿索菲亚曾拍出电影史上最具印象深刻（且风格迥异）的两份电影作品年表，在电影媒介上留下了不可磨灭的印记（她的儿子罗曼〔Roman〕的事业也同样不容小觑）。同样，索菲亚和科波拉家族对埃莉诺的作品也深感骄傲，这些作品涵盖了极其广泛的纪实表达。埃莉诺兼具视频日记创作者、多媒体艺术家、回忆录作家以及电影导演等多重身份，她始终在不断雕琢自己的艺术遗产与影像履历，而这往往是以捕捉她所爱之人在工作中的状态为名的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "和她的家人一样，作为一名电影人兼纪录片导演，她在艺术上绝不妥协——而她的遗作《制作〈绝代艳后〉》（Making Marie Antoinette）正是最明晰的证明。我们从影片中无拘无束的视角以及对一切近距离、个人化事物的毫不掩饰的记录中，见证了极其典型的埃莉诺·科波拉式创作方法。如果电影片场是一台机器，她就是其中那个独自漂浮、四处游荡的齿轮，不属于任何地方，却又在所有地方都能找到归属感。但她的最后这部电影还有另一个元素，让它带有一种感伤的、圈内人般的视角。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "2020年，随着大流行骤然降临，母女二人开始着手整理埃莉诺2005年在索菲亚的《绝代艳后》（Marie Antoinette）片场拍摄的80多个小时的素材。当埃莉诺于2024年离世时，索菲亚接过了火炬，将母亲的最后一部电影带向终点。正因如此，《制作〈绝代艳后〉》比埃莉诺以往的幕后项目更加聚焦于她母亲在片场那具有感染力的存在感与内心世界，它将母亲在每日日记中的画外音与埃莉诺当天拍摄的素材完美交织。与其说《制作〈绝代艳后〉》仅仅是捕捉运转中的机器，不如说它通过女儿的镜头，为埃莉诺提供了一种更具自我反思、沉思以及充满爱意的审视。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在该片上映之际，我们与她坐下来进行了一次访谈，聊了聊作为家族生意的电影制作、母亲在片场的身影、在银幕上看到自己的奇异体验，以及她在过去20年里职业生涯的演变。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《电影舞台》：当你接手时，你妈妈已经完成了多少剪辑？你又是如何带着对她的设想来指导剪辑工作的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "索菲亚·科波拉：她当时正准备审阅素材，但我们还没开始剪辑。那本该是我们一起做的事。她有个当剪辑师的朋友，她本来想和对方一起合作。但我们实际上并未开始剪辑，当时正处于审阅阶段。所以我一直在跟她过素材，她也在向我解释她被哪些部分所吸引。后来在她去世后，我找到了这位剪辑师，并试着去弄清楚如何按照她想要的方式、按照我们曾讨论过的方式把它完成。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你们讨论这件事有多久了？我知道片中提到你们俩是在2020年开始着手处理的，但从2020年到2024年，关于这部电影的讨论有多频繁？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当时我们只是在审阅素材，并探讨一个问题：它能成为一部电影吗？这也是她一直在问的。因为这从来就不是为了拍成电影而拍的。我当时并没有意识到她有这么多的素材，也就是在那时我们开始浏览这些素材。后来花了一些时间才真正确定团队以及我们要如何推进。而在过去这一年里，我们一直在剪辑它。我是通过我妈妈的一个朋友认识剪辑师亚伦·马修斯（Aaron Matthews）的，我以前从未和他合作过，所以对我来说这是一个全新的过程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "观看这部电影对你来说是一种什么样的体验？它有点像发烧梦一般的感觉吗？还是充满怀旧？亦或是很有压力？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你有没有告诉过她某些你想让她拍的内容，还是说她总是按自己的想法去拍？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我当时忙着赶进度完成每天的拍摄，而且我知道她眼光极好、总能捕捉到有趣的细节，所以我很高兴她想拍什么就拍什么。我作为纪录片导演很尊重她，我知道她很喜欢米莱娜（Milena）和服装，所以我知道这是她真正热爱的东西。后来看素材时，我看到了很多以前从未见过的东西，因为我当时在前主景。我甚至不知道有成里长的服装和假发给临时演员准备，我连那个区域都没去过。所以去发现这些真的很让人开心。", true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《绝代艳后》（Marie Antoinette）是你迄今为止规模最大的一次拍摄。在观看这部片子时，你对这段经历有什么反思？这种规模和预算是你以后还想再次尝试的，还是觉得做一次就够了？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
In April 2024, Sofia Coppola lost her mother, Eleanor. The “cool” (as Sofia describes her), anchoral matriarch of the Coppola family was as proud a mother as she was a wife, her husband Francis and daughter Sofia having mounted two of the most impressive (and unalike) filmographies in the history of cinema, leaving an indelible mark on the medium (her son Roman’s career nothing to balk at either). Likewise, Sofia and the Coppolas were equally proud of Eleanor’s work, which covers a vast range of chronicling expressions. Part video diarist, part multimedia artist, part memoirist, part film director, and more, Eleanor was always chipping away at her own legacy, her own filmography, often in the name of capturing her loved ones at work.

Like her family, she was artistically uncompromising as a filmmaker/documentarian, and Making Marie Antoinette —her final, posthumous film—shows us exactly how. We witness the quintessential Eleanor Coppola approach in the unfettered access to and unapologetic documentation of everything up close and personal. If the film set is a machine, she’s the lone free-floating, nomadic cog, not belonging anywhere but finding a sense of belonging everywhere. But there’s another element to her last movie that gives it a sentimental, inside-baseball perspective.

In 2020, with the pandemic freshly upon us, mother and daughter began shaping the 80+ hours of footage Eleanor had shot on the set of Sofia’s Marie Antoinette in 2005. When Eleanor passed in 2024, Sofia took up the torch to see her mother’s final film to the finish line. As a result, Making Marie Antoinette hones in on her mother’s contagious presence and inner life on set much more than Eleanor’s past behind-the-scenes projects had, combining the voiceover of her mother in daily diary entries in concert with the footage Eleanor shot that day. Instead of merely capturing the machine at work, Making Marie Antoinette offers a more self-reflective, contemplative, and adoring look at Eleanor through the lens of her daughter.

On the heels of the film’s release, we sat down to talk to her about filmmaking as a family affair, her mother’s presence on set, the strange experience of watching herself onscreen, and how her career has evolved in the last twenty years.

The Film Stage: How much of the edit had your mom finished when you took over, and how did you approach directing the edit with her in mind?

Sofia Coppola: She had just been reviewing the footage, but we hadn’t started editing. That was something we were going to do together. She had a friend that was an editor that she wanted to start working on it. But we didn’t actually start the edit, we were just kind of in the review process. So I was going through it with her, and she was explaining what parts she was drawn to. And then I found the editor after she passed and tried to figure out how to finish it in the way she would want it, how we were talking about it.

How long had you been talking about it? I know in the film it says that you both started working on it in 2020, but how active was the conversation about the film between 2020 and 2024?

At that time we were just reviewing the footage and the idea of: could it be a film, which is what she was asking. Because it was never intended to be a film. And I didn’t realize she had so much footage, and that’s when we started looking through it. And then it took a while to actually figure out the team and how we were going to do it. Then this past year, we’ve been editing it, and I met Aaron Matthews, the editor, through a friend of my mom’s, and I’d never worked with him, so it was a whole new process for me.

What is your experience like watching the film? Is it fever-dream-esque? Nostalgic? Stressful?

Yeah, it’s really weird to go back to that time. I mean, I love seeing Jason [Schwartzman] and Kirsten [Dunst] and being on that set without the stress of being in the moment of it. Like, to have some distance. But I do get a little stressed watching it. Like, that feeling of those days on set, how intense it was. And it’s cringy for me to see myself.

In what sense? What makes you cringe?

Just to see myself on camera being a young director, not quite as comfortable being assertive about things. And, like, when I’m irritable. I’m vulnerable in a way that I would never be with a normal behind-the-scenes crew. And I hope there’s always something valuable about a personal look at someone creative. But, as far as being the subject of it, that part’s hard. But I really relied on the editor to be like, “Okay, what do we keep in here?”

When you watch yourself on set, are there specific things that you wish you could go back and do differently?

Now I’m more experienced and I’m more comfortable asking for what I want. I hope for young filmmakers, they see it’s a process and an evolution, that you don’t just show up one day as a fully-formed, experienced person. But there’s things like when we were shooting the big opera scene and we’re changing the extras. And now, as an experienced person, I’m like, “Nobody’s going to notice that the extras weren’t wearing the same costumes in an opera scene thirty minutes later,” you know? [Laughs]. Like, just move them around. We’re all stressing about changing the wigs of the extras. So there are just things that over time you learn. You can get away with a lot.

How did the diaristic element come in, where we’re going through your mom’s diary? Was that something she had put in there or that you added in?

At the end of her life, she wanted her journals, this last book, published. It was third in her book series. So that was something we were also working on at the same time. And the editor helped find the passages that connected to the set. We weren’t originally sure how we were going to put this together. And then luckily, those passages connected with the footage, and so we found that we could make a narration out of it and tie it together.

I know that your parents have been on your sets regularly from the beginning and that you grew up on your dad’s sets, but at the same time, they’re still your parents. Was it ever strange to just have your mom walking around on set with a camera sort of up in your grill?

I’m kind of used to it. So yeah, sometimes. Like when Kirsten and I are trying to gossip and I have my microphone on and I don’t want my mom hearing that conversation. But for the most part, I grew up on set and with her shooting, so I kind of just go with that part of the atmosphere on set. And it was nice to have my mom there, because she was so into it. She’s so encouraging and loved seeing what was all being put together, so it was fun to share that with an enthusiastic mom present.

Did you ever tell her certain things you wanted her to shoot or was she always going off her own directive?

I was just so busy trying to get our days done, and I knew that she had such a great eye that zeros in on interesting details, so I was just happy for her to shoot whatever she thought was interesting. I respect her as a documentarian, and I knew that she loved Milena [Canonero] and the costumes, so I knew that was something she was really into. And then seeing the footage, I saw a lot of things that I had never seen, because I was on the main set. I didn’t realize there were miles of wigs for the extras. I hadn’t even been in that area. So it’s fun to discover.

Marie Antoinette is the biggest shoot of your career to date. What are your reflections on that as you’re watching it? Is that size and budget something you would ever want to do again or are you, like, one and done?

I think at the end I was so fed up I said I’d never do it again, and I don’t feel the same way now, but I definitely learned that I like working in a more hands-on, intimate way. I just think I had that kind of youthful naivete. You take on something without realizing what it really is. I don’t think I’d be as bold now, maybe, but who knows? That’s part of being a creative person—you’re always trying to push things and do things you haven’t done before.

Was it an emotional experience taking up this project? And how did you decide to do that?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I just felt like my mom wanted it done, so I felt like I was on a mission, like I had to complete this for her. And, in a way, it was a gift that she gave this to me, this footage of this time in my life that I got to revisit and see through her point of view and take the time to complete something for her and spend this time in her work and her point of view. So yeah, it was a big undertaking and emotional.

I didn’t realize how long it would take, and it really took me the [last] year. I didn’t realize how much I had to get into this mode and couldn’t really focus on my other work—to really just take this time. But I’m glad that I did. I’m happy that it’s completed and coming out in the world, because she really wanted it to be done. And the anniversary of Marie Antoinette was our deadline, because it took a while, so we were like, “We have to finish it!” It gave us something to work towards. Otherwise, I don’t know when it would’ve gotten done.

This is also your second documentary in a row after not having worked in documentaries. Is that something you’re interested in continuing more?

It was interesting to just do something different, but now I really miss making a narrative. Getting to imagine a world and create it, because it’s so fun to work with my team and make a world. So I’m looking forward to getting back to my usual thing.

Do you have projects that are currently in production?

No. Now with this finished, I’ll get back to thinking about what’s next. But I’m not sure.

While you were working on Making Marie Antoinette , was your dad ever part of the process? Even if it was just talking about your mom and how she might want something to be edited or put?

Not really, but I showed him. I always show him a rough cut, because he’s so smart about editing and has an opinion, and I value that. But he wasn’t so directly involved. I showed him some cuts. I [actually] showed a lot of cuts to a friend of my mom’s just to be reminded of her perspective and how she would want it. So that helped.

Making Marie Antoinette is now in theaters and arrives on MUBI on November 6. The new 4K restoration of Marie Antoinette is now on MUBI.

article_text:
Going on two years after the wildfires that devastated Pacific Palisades and other Los Angeles-area neighborhoods, a popular moviehouse is ready for its closeup. Paramount Pictures and real estate developer Rick Caruso said Tuesday that the Bay Theater in Palisades Village will reopen before year’s end.

Related Stories

Celebrities Who Lost Their Homes In The Los Angeles Wildfires

Discovery+ Raises Prices In One Of Skydance’s First Streaming Moves After Merger Close

The high-end five-screen venue at 1035 N. Swarthmore Ave., shuttered since the Palisades Fire in early January 2025, is being restored, and luxury cinema operator The Lot will manage it. Along with first-run movies and classics, the Bay will host special screenings and immersive theatrical experiences, said Paramount, which is taking over the theater formerly operated by Netflix and Cinepolis before that.

“Together with Caruso, we are proud to help bring the Bay back to life as a place for the Pacific Palisades community to gather around the shared experience of cinema,” said David Ellison, chairman and CEO of Skydance. “This theater has always meant more than movies alone — it’s woven into the fabric of this neighborhood, and helping restore it is a privilege. We’re inspired by the resilience of Pacific Palisades residents, and we’re honored to help support this community’s comeback.”

Watch on Deadline

The surrounding Caruso-owned Palisades Village reopened during the summer, and now the Bay Theater is set open its doors by the end of 2026, though no date is set.

The original Bay Theater opened down the road on Sunset Boulevard in 1949 before closing in 1978. The venue’s current iteration debuted in 2018.

“The Bay has always been at the heart of the Palisades,” said Caruso, who was runner-up in the race for Los Angeles mayor in 2022, “and its return is one of the most meaningful signs yet that this community … is coming back stronger than ever.”

The Lot, which will oversee operations for the Bay, runs luxury dine-in theaters in La Jolla, Newport Beach and other California cities.

title_original: Riitta Päiväläinen
editorial_title_zh: Riitta Päiväläinen
editorial_excerpt_zh: Phantasma系列 “自然是我的想象力游乐场，在这里不可能也能变为可能。” 在Phantasma系列中，我的视觉语言走向想象、梦境与 […] Cet article Riitta Päiväläinen est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Phantasma系列", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“自然是我的想象力游乐场，在这里不可能也能变为可能。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在Phantasma系列中，我的视觉语言走向想象、梦境与幻想。自1998年以来，在单一创作视野的引导下，我的艺术作品深入探讨了记忆、过去与自然之间错综复杂的关系。通过我的作品，我探索潜意识、童年、替代与潜在的叙事、共同的集体情感、联想以及内在自我。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的创作过程总是从寻找一个能启发灵感的地方开始；风景本身邀请我去构建独特的、特定场地的织物装置，然后将其拍摄下来。我深深地被无人居住、具有隐秘感且没有任何经济价值的环境所吸引。对我来说，自然的意义在于人类将其视为创造力和想象力源泉的能力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一次，我的旅程将我带到了拉普兰和冰岛寂静、未驯服的风景中，在那里，自然剥去了不必要的一切，只留下最本质的东西：石头、冰、风和光。对我来说，这种荒凉并不空洞——它是一个极美之所，也是潜意识的画布。这些地方犹如心理心境风景、特定场地的布景，以及人类心灵、童年记忆和内在心理的隐喻。通过聚焦这些脆弱、未受触及的领地，我的作品成为了对自然无声的呐喊——一种尊重和保护未驯服世界的诗意呼吁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Phantasma系列延续了我长期以来以风景、地点、二手衣物、丝带和织物为媒介的摄影实践。在风景之中，服装形成了类似人形、精灵或幽灵的形状——在观者、风景和无形之物之间创造了一场凄美、想象中的相遇与对话。风景中的一块织物仅仅是一个起点。通过这个过程，人们可以以一种全新方式去感知寻常风景。通过精确构图、选择完美的光线与氛围并塑造织物，我寻求的是物质与地点之间的平衡与互动。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一个完全由女性独立完成的项目，我总是在荒野的寂静中独自工作。独处使我能够直面内心的自我，专注于本质，并让想象力得以延伸。这种孤独的过程为我的工作设定了明确的界限，迫使我完全依赖自己的直觉和力量。在自然的规则下工作意味着适应不可预测的情况——驾驭天气、风和光的突然变化，这些都在积极塑造着每件作品的成果。在这些紧张的时刻，我独自完成这个缓慢过程的每一步，用大画幅野外相机将这些稍纵即逝的相遇记录在4×5英寸的胶片上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我特别对共同的集体情感感兴趣，以及如何通过艺术手段传达深邃、无言的感受。我追求的是一种物理上并不存在但在观者心中被唤醒的生存与情感层面，它由观者的个人历史和经历所塑造。对我来说，最终影像所传达的情感共鸣始终与画面中的物理主体一样至关重要——甚至可能更为重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在古老的岩石之中，“水的守护者”浮现了——低语着即使在最崎岖的地形中，也存在着一种隐蔽的、保护性的优雅。Phantasma邀请人们去超越可见之物，在那里，大自然的严酷与梦想的温柔相遇。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "www.riittapaivalainen.com", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "精选奖项： • 2020年 – LensCulture曝光奖，入围及评委优选 • 2011年 – 威廉·蒂林奖，芬兰美术协会", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Phantasma Series"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Nature is my imaginary playground where the impossible becomes possible.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the Phantasma series, my visual language moves toward imagination, dreams, and fantasy. Guided by a singular creative vision since 1998, my artistic work delves into the intricate relationships between memory, the past, and nature. article_text:
Phantasma Series

“Nature is my imaginary playground where the impossible becomes possible.”

In the Phantasma series, my visual language moves toward imagination, dreams, and fantasy. Guided by a singular creative vision since 1998, my artistic work delves into the intricate relationships between memory, the past, and nature. Through my work, I delve into the subconscious, childhood, alternative and potential narratives, shared collective emotions, associations, and the inner self.

My creative process always begins with the search for a place that inspires me; the landscape itself invites me to build unique, site-specific fabric installations, which I then photograph. I am deeply drawn to uninhabited, secluded environments that hold no economic value. For me, the significance of nature lies in the human capacity to see it as a source of creation and imagination.

This time, my journey has led me to the silent, untamed landscapes of Lapland and Iceland, where nature strips away the unnecessary, leaving only the essential: stone, ice, wind, and light. To me, this barrenness is not empty—it is a space of extreme beauty and a canvas for the subconscious. These places work as psychological mindscapes, site-specific mise-en-scènes, and metaphors for the human mind, childhood memories, and internal psychology. By focusing on these fragile, untouched territories, my work serves as a silent advocacy for nature—a poetic plea to respect and protect the untamed world.

The Phantasma series builds upon my long-standing photographic practice of working with landscape, place, second-hand clothing, ribbons and fabrics. Within the scenery, the garments form shapes resembling human figures, spirits, or ghosts—creating a poignant, imaginary meeting and a dialogue between the viewer, the landscape, and the invisible. A mere fabric in the scenery is only a starting point. Through this process, an everyday landscape can be perceived in an entirely new way. By precisely framing the landscape, choosing the perfect light and atmosphere, and sculpting the fabric, I seek a balance and interaction between the material and the place.

Operating entirely as a one-woman project, I always work alone in the silence of the wilderness. Being alone enables me to face my inner self, focus on the essential, and allow my imagination to expand. This solitary process sets clear boundaries for my work, forcing me to rely entirely on my intuition and strength. Working on nature’s terms means adapting to the unpredictable—navigating sudden shifts in weather, wind, and light, which actively shape the outcome of each work. In these intense moments, I carry out every step of this slow process, capturing these fleeting encounters on 4×5-inch film with a large format field camera.

I am especially interested in shared collective emotions and how to convey profound, wordless feelings through artistic means. I seek a layer of existence and emotion that is not physically present but awakened in the viewer’s mind, shaped by their personal history and experiences. For me, the emotional resonance conveyed by the final image is always as vital—maybe even more so—than the physical subject matter within the frame.

Among the ancient rocks, The Guardian of Water emerged—whispering that even in the most rugged terrain, there is a hidden, protective grace. Phantasma invites one to see beyond the visible, where the harshness of nature meets the softness of a dream.
